options.text: Create a dedicated checks workspace and set its spending limit. Use `agent_with_overrides` to change `model` only for test sessions, leaving regular checks on the existing agent.

Move regular checks to a scheduled deployment with `budget.max_list_cost: "3000"` (USD). Immediately update the agent’s `model` for replacement testing so all later checks use the new version; revert if problems occur.

Move regular checks to a scheduled deployment with budget `"3000"` (USD). Archive sessions that reach the cap and start new ones with the same instructions; test the replacement with `agent_with_overrides` sessions.

Move regular checks to a scheduled deployment with budget `"3000"` (USD). After reviewing a `budget_reached` pause, raise the budget above spend to resume, and first validate the replacement through `agent_with_overrides` test sessions.

questions.explanation:
Managed Agents session budgets stop new model requests when public-list-price session spending reaches `max_list_cost`, an integer-cent string. A capped session becomes idle with `stop_reason: budget_reached`, preserving history and sandbox rather than terminating. Raising the budget above spend or removing it automatically resumes the session. Deployment budgets are copied to each session, applying per run rather than cumulatively. A `model` override through `agent_with_overrides` applies only to that session without changing the agent or creating a version; updating the agent's configuration creates a new version. The decisive requirements are per-check caps, same-state resumption, no report-API impact, partial testing first, and unchanged regular checks during testing.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: A separate workspace protects reporting, and testing is correct, but workspace limits apply to total workspace usage rather than individual checks. At the limit, requests receive 400 errors rather than a resumable budget pause.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Per-run caps are correct, but updating the agent creates a version and immediately changes regular checks too, violating partial-first testing and unchanged production configuration. Reverting after problems is not a substitute for prior testing.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Caps and testing are correct, but archived sessions accept no new events, and new sessions do not inherit the old conversation and sandbox state.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Per-run budgets, state-preserving pause/resume, and session-scoped model trials satisfy all five conditions. After testing, update the agent so regular checks migrate before retirement.

Additional note: Budget checks occur between model requests, so the last request may slightly exceed the cap; allow headroom. Deployment run records include the agent `version`, enabling verification after updates. Migrate all usage before retirement to avoid failed requests afterward.

**References**: [Session budgets › When a session reaches its budget](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/budgets) · [Session budgets › Resume a session at its budget](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/budgets) · [Session budgets › Budgets on deployments](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/budgets) · [Start a session › Override agent configuration for a session](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/sessions) · [Define your agent › Update an agent](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/agent-setup) · [Session operations › Archiving a session](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/session-operations) · [Rate limits › Spend limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) · [Model deprecations › Migrating to replacements](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations)

questions.title: Structuring helpdesk inquiries with different processing branches
questions.prompt:
An internal helpdesk wants an agent to handle employee inquiries. Inquiries fall into billing, accounts, and technical support, each with distinct instructions and tools: settlement lookup, permission-change requests, and incident-log search respectively. Offline evaluation shows sufficiently accurate preliminary classification of branch and difficulty (simple/complex). Requirements:

- Expose **only the branch-specific instructions and tools** during processing.
- Use **small models** for simple inquiries to reduce cost.
- Fix model calls at **exactly two per inquiry** for predictable latency.

Which architecture best fits?

options.text: Classify branch and difficulty first, then make one processing call with that branch's instructions/tools and a model tier appropriate to difficulty.
Classify only the branch, then make one processing call with its instructions/tools, using the same large model regardless of difficulty.
Classify branch and difficulty, run branch-specific processing, then review every answer in another call and rerun processing if it falls below the threshold.
Give one agent all three toolsets and branch instructions; let it repeatedly select and call tools, starting simple inquiries on a small model.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's agent-design article recommends routing for complex tasks with distinct categories best handled differently: classify inputs and send them to category-specific downstream prompts and tools. It also gives routing easy questions to smaller models as an example. Classification can use an LLM or traditional classifier if sufficiently accurate. All four options can process inquiries, but the incorrect choices each violate a constraint. The decisive requirements are [small models for cost savings] and [exactly two model calls].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: One classification determines branch and difficulty, selecting instructions, tools, and model tier for the second call and satisfying all three requirements. Tradeoffs are misclassification causing the wrong branch/tier and maintaining classification rules plus dedicated configurations as branches grow.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It preserves dedicated configurations and two calls but uses a large model regardless of difficulty, violating [small models for cost savings].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It preserves branch configuration and model tier, but mandatory review and possible reprocessing violate [exactly two calls].
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It branches to smaller models but exposes all toolsets, violating [dedicated tools only], and variable repeated calls violate fixed call count. It is excessive for inquiries with predetermined subtasks.

**References**: [Building effective agents › Workflow: Routing](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [Building effective agents › Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

questions.title: Translation improvement through critique and stopping criteria
questions.prompt:
A translation team wants higher literary-translation quality. Human feedback on style preservation and glossary compliance noticeably improves translations, and a critique LLM given the documented criteria produces similar feedback. Requirements:

- Critique feedback must **feed back into the translation**.
- **Avoid unnecessary calls** once the threshold score is reached.
- Translation and critique calls combined must **not exceed six per manuscript**.

Which structure best fits?

options.text: Translate the same source three times in parallel and vote for sentences with the most overlap.
Use a fixed three-call chain of translation, critique, and revision, always returning the third result regardless of score.
Repeat translation and critique while scores improve, stopping when they decrease, without a separate call limit.
Loop translation and critique, stopping when the score reaches the threshold and enforcing a hard maximum of six total calls.

questions.explanation:
The evaluator-optimizer pattern iterates between one LLM generating output and another evaluating and providing feedback. Documentation recommends it when evaluation criteria are clear, human feedback demonstrably improves quality, and an LLM can provide similar feedback; literary translation is an example. All options produce translations, but incorrect ones violate individual requirements: [feedback loop], [no unnecessary calls after threshold], and [six-call maximum].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Parallel voting repeats work to increase confidence, but free-form translation has no stage feeding critique back into revision, violating [feedback loop].
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It incorporates feedback within the cap, but runs all three calls even when the first translation meets the threshold, violating [no unnecessary calls after threshold].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Continuing while scores improve reduces waste, but sustained improvement may exceed six calls, violating [six-call maximum].
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Threshold-based stopping plus a hard cap satisfies all three requirements. The tradeoff is that capped cases may remain below threshold and must be flagged for human review.

**References**: [Building effective agents › Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [Building effective agents › Workflow: Parallelization](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

questions.title: Choosing an architecture for variable-length support involving refunds
questions.prompt:
A customer-support team is building a conversational agent using order-lookup, refund, and ticket-update tools. A case may end after one lookup or extend across dozens of turns with customer questions and additional lookups. Refunds are irreversible and erroneous refunds incur substantial losses. Requirements:

- Steps and counts **depend on customer answers**, so code cannot prescribe a fixed sequence.
- Refund-execution errors must be **effectively zero**, with reproducible execution rationale for later review.
- Non-refund-stage p95 latency must **not exceed its current level**.
- There are **two operations engineers**.

Which architecture best fits?

options.text: Let a single tool-equipped agent lead the conversation, while refund execution requires code validation of order state and limits followed by human approval.
Code a fixed order-lookup → refund-eligibility → refund-execution → ticket-update workflow, with a separate LLM call per step.
Classify inquiries into lookup, refund, and ticket specialist agents, each directly executing its own tools without approval.
Have an orchestrator spawn subagents per case for parallel lookup and refund review, then combine results and execute refunds itself.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's agent-design article identifies customer support as suitable for agents because conversational flow needs external data and actions, including refunds and ticket updates. Agents nevertheless incur cost and compounding-error risks, warranting sandbox testing and guardrails; its multi-agent article reports roughly 15 times chat's token usage. Incorrect architectures each violate one of [customer-dependent steps], [effectively zero refund errors], [non-refund p95], or [two engineers].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: An agent handles open-ended dialogue while irreversible refunds alone receive deterministic code checks and human approval. The tradeoffs are refund approval delay and approval staffing, which the prompt permits by limiting the p95 requirement to non-refund stages.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It deterministically controls refunds, but cannot fit lookup-only or repeated-clarification cases into a fixed sequence, violating [customer-dependent steps].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Routing helps distinct categories and allows flexibility, but unapproved refund execution cannot ensure [effectively zero refund errors]; operating three agents also adds overhead.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: Parallel lookup may accelerate some work, but multi-agent token and coordination costs conflict with [non-refund p95] and [two engineers]. It also lacks a separate pre-refund validation gate.

**References**: [Building effective agents › Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [Building effective agents › Appendix 1: Agents in practice](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [How we built our multi-agent research system › Token usage](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)

questions.title: Task characteristics that suit parallel multi-agent research
questions.prompt: A competitor-intelligence reporting team is considering parallel research subagents. Each report has high business value, so **substantially higher token cost is acceptable**. Choose **two** characteristics that make a task suitable for a multi-agent architecture.

options.text: Research directions are independent, so agents can explore them concurrently without exchanging intermediate results.
Agents must continually share identical context, with many dependencies where one subtask's output feeds another.
The task edits several tightly coupled code files simultaneously, allowing one editor agent per file.
Most work is simple fact-checking answered by one search, with response speed paramount.
The information to gather exceeds one agent's context window.
Minimizing token cost is the highest priority, and there are only two or three subtasks.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's multi-agent research article identifies suitable work as breadth-first queries pursuing independent directions, large-scale parallelism, and information exceeding one context window. Shared-context requirements, extensive inter-agent dependencies, and most coding tasks with little parallelizable work are poor fits. Multi-agent systems use roughly 15 times chat's tokens, so task value must justify this. The prompt's [higher cost acceptable] premise helps distinguish the alternatives.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Concurrent independent exploration is a principal documented fit. Its advantage disappears if independence fails.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Documentation explicitly identifies this as unsuitable: sharing context creates coordination overhead exceeding separation benefits.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Coupled code edits offer limited parallelism, and agents editing shared files need coordination. Most coding tasks are less parallelizable than research.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, appropriate for a different situation)**: A single call or agent suffices for simple facts; there is insufficient value to justify extra multi-agent cost and latency.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: When information exceeds one window, subagents exploring in separate fresh contexts and returning summaries provide an advantage.
- **{{option:F}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Roughly 15 times token usage runs counter to cost minimization and contradicts the prompt's cost-tolerance premise.

**References**: [How we built our multi-agent research system › Token usage and when multi-agent fits](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) · [Building effective agents › Workflow: Parallelization](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

questions.title: Controlling spend from excessive Opus 5 subagent spawning
questions.prompt:
A repository-auditing team using the Claude Agent SDK sees spending spikes after upgrading to Claude Opus 5, which spawns subagents much more often. Audits are independent by service, making parallel subagents valuable. Each subagent response costs at most approximately $1. Requirements:

- Total spend per query **must not exceed $40**, enforced by the **runtime**, not prompt instructions.
- Retain **parallel execution benefits**, with multiple concurrent subagents.
- Subagents must retain the **higher-tier model** for audit quality.
- Leaving some services unaudited after hitting the limit is **acceptable**.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Instruct the system prompt to use at most five subagents and spend no more than $40; check compliance in retrospective cost reports.
Set `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` to 1 and `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` to 5, lower subagent `maxTurns`, but set no spending option.
Limit depth to 1 and concurrent subagents to 5 through environment variables, and set `max_budget_usd` to $30, below the $40 ceiling.
Change subagent `model` to a smaller model and `effort` to `"low"` to reduce unit cost, retaining default depth and concurrency.

questions.explanation:
Agent SDK documentation says subagents can spawn further subagents, growing one prompt into a tree. It recommends limits for depth (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH`, default 3), concurrency (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`, default 20), and spend (`max_budget_usd`). Opus 5 delegates eagerly, making these important; instructions only guide behavior and should be paired with configuration. Budget checks occur after responses arrive, allowing overshoot from the response crossing the cap and additional spending by already-running subagents. The decisive requirements are [runtime enforcement], [no more than $40], and [retain higher-tier model].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Instructions alone rely on model compliance, violating [runtime enforcement]. Retrospective reporting reveals rather than prevents overspending.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It limits fan-out, but `maxTurns` counts tool-use round trips, not total spend. Sequential new subagents across many services can still exceed $40.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Environment variables enforce structural limits and a query option enforces spend. Five concurrent agents at about $1 per response imply approximately $6 overshoot around the $30 cap, remaining under $40. Tradeoffs are slower audits from reducing concurrency 20→5 and unfinished services when the cap is reached.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Lower unit cost does not cap total volume with unchanged depth/concurrency, and the smaller model violates [retain higher-tier model].

Also note: Documented subagent enforcement of these variables and budget applies from TypeScript SDK v0.3.219 and Python SDK v0.2.127, corresponding to Claude Code v2.1.219 or later.

**References**: [Subagents in the SDK › Cap subagent depth, concurrency, and spend](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents) · [How the agent loop works › Turns and budget](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop)

questions.title: Deciding whether to split a single agent
questions.prompt:
A team builds a shopping-support agent with the OpenAI Agents SDK for Python. One agent handles order lookup, shipping guidance, FAQs, and refunds. The first three share lookup tools and response policy. Refunds alone have a different policy and powerful tools, and lengthy refund instructions destabilize general answers. Requirements:

- Expose refund policy and tools **only during refund handling**.
- **Remove** refund policy from general-inquiry prompts.
- Add agents, traces, and approval points **only where separation provides value**.
- Keep an LLM interpreting refund policy in light of customer circumstances.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Keep one agent, summarize refund policy to shorten the prompt, and always expose the refund tool with a description saying to call it only for refunds.
Add only a refund specialist with refund policy/tools; keep the other three tasks with the existing agent.
Create separate order, shipping, FAQ, and refund agents, with a classifier handing inquiries to the appropriate one.
Remove refunds from the agent and use a fixed form/rules engine, with the agent forwarding only refund-intake information.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's orchestration guide recommends starting with one agent where possible and adding specialists only for material benefits in capability/policy isolation, prompt clarity, or trace readability, such as a branch requiring genuinely different instructions, tools, or policies. Each additional agent also adds prompts, traces, and approval points. Incorrect options violate [refund-only exposure], [separate only for value], or [LLM continues refund-policy interpretation].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It is structurally simplest, but always exposes refund tools and retains summarized refund policy in general prompts, violating [refund-only exposure].
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Only refunds, whose policy and authority differ, are isolated; their tools/instructions stay with the specialist. Keeping the other tasks together minimizes agents. The tradeoff is designing handoff or calling between the agents and adding a refund approval point.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: It isolates refunds but unnecessarily splits three tasks sharing tools and policy, violating [separate only for value] and adding prompts, traces, and approvals.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It isolates refunds but assigns policy interpretation to a rules engine, violating [LLM continues refund-policy interpretation].

**References**: [Agent orchestration (OpenAI Agents guide)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/orchestration) · [Handoffs (OpenAI Agents SDK)](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/)

questions.title: Delegation when parallel code review needs internal function tools
questions.prompt:
An internal platform team uses the OpenAI Agents API beta to review dozens of independent modules in parallel, with a coordinator assigning modules to subagents. Some reviews need the **current settlement state** of an internal billing system, available only through a **function tool** executed on an internal server. Requirements:

- Parallel module review must finish within a **three-hour overnight window**.
- Settlement state must be **current at review time**.
- **No new servers, including MCP servers**, may be built this quarter.
- Review subagents are read-only and do not edit files.

Which design best fits?

options.text: Download settlement state to an environment file before the nightly run and let subagents read it during parallel reviews.
Build an internal MCP server wrapping settlement lookup, configure it for subagents, and let them query directly during parallel reviews.
Use only the coordinator to review modules sequentially and directly call the function tool whenever settlement lookup is needed.
Let subagents review modules in parallel and report settlement-lookup needs; the coordinator calls the function tool and returns results.

questions.explanation:
Agents API multi-agent documentation says the main agent coordinates subagents and combines results; subagents do not support function tools. They can use configured MCP tools, web search, and environment files/command-line tools, with default concurrency of six. Function tools require application handlers to execute calls and return results, so those steps must remain with the coordinator. The decisive requirements are [function-tool-only lookup], [current values], [no new server], and [three-hour window].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Environment files support parallel review without new servers, but pre-run snapshots are not current at review time, violating [current values].
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: MCP support preserves parallelism and freshness, but building/operating an MCP server violates [no new server].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The coordinator can obtain current values through function tools, but sequential review lacks the parallelism needed for [three-hour window].
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Reviews remain parallel while only function-tool lookups stay with the coordinator, satisfying all four conditions. Tradeoffs are serialized lookup bottlenecks, larger coordinator context, and additional request/response coordination with subagents.

Also note: Documentation says agents editing the same files must coordinate changes; read-only review avoids that issue. Agents API requires the beta header `agents=v1`.

**References**: [Multi-agent (OpenAI Agents API)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/multi-agent) · [Architecture (OpenAI Agents API)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/architecture)

questions.title: Why begin an agent project with direct API calls?
questions.prompt: A new agent-project team has no prior agent-building experience. Its first milestone is a simple loop with just two tool calls working **within two weeks**. The team wants to debug by directly inspecting the exact prompts and responses exchanged with the model. Which starting approach best fits?

options.text: Implement the loop with direct model API calls, introducing a framework only after a clear need emerges.
Start with a popular agent framework and rely on default prompt templates and tool connections.
Start with a framework, spending week one studying its source to understand hidden prompts and response handling before implementing features.
Begin with a multi-agent template for future expansion and connect only two agents for this milestone.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's agent-design article recommends starting with direct LLM API calls because many patterns require only a few lines of code. Framework abstraction can obscure actual prompts/responses, complicate debugging, and encourage unnecessary complexity. Even when using a framework, its internals should be understood. The decisive requirements are [debug exact prompts/responses] and [two weeks, simple loop].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Exposed prompts/responses and a simple loop fit the milestone. The tradeoff is implementing shared features such as retries and logging yourself.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It starts quickly but defaults obscure prompts/responses, violating [debug exact prompts/responses].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Understanding internals follows the documentation's caveat, but spending the first week on source analysis pressures [simple loop within two weeks], an unnecessary cost with direct calls.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: Future expansion may sound reasonable, but multi-agent architecture adds unnecessary complexity to a two-tool-call loop. Documentation recommends the simplest solution first.

**References**: [Building effective agents › Frameworks](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [Building effective agents › Summary](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

questions.title: Combining fixed-order stages and parallel retrieval in ADK
questions.prompt:
A document-processing pipeline uses Google ADK. Requirements:

- Summarization, translation, and review must **always run in that order**.
- Retrieval from three independent sources must run **concurrently**, with all three results **combined into one** for the next stage.

Choose **two** configurations that satisfy these requirements.

options.text: Make summarization, translation, and review subagents of a coordinator that dynamically selects the next agent according to instructions.
Place summarization, translation, and review under `SequentialAgent` in that order.
Place the three retrieval agents under `LoopAgent`, retrieving one source per iteration and collecting results in the final iteration.
Place retrieval agents under `ParallelAgent`, store each result in a different `output_key`, then have a merge agent read and combine them.
Place retrieval agents under `ParallelAgent` and concatenate outputs in arrival order without a merge stage before forwarding them.
Place all summarization, translation, review, and retrieval agents in one `ParallelAgent`, running everything simultaneously and collecting results.

questions.explanation:
ADK template workflows provide fixed sequential, looping, and parallel execution. `SequentialAgent` runs subagents in order. `ParallelAgent` runs them concurrently without guaranteed result order or automatic sharing of branch conversation history/state during execution. Documentation illustrates storing branch outputs under separate `output_key` values and reading them in a subsequent merge agent. The decisive requirements are [always this order], [concurrent execution], and [combined output].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Dynamic coordinator choice is flexible but depends on model judgment and cannot guarantee [always this order].
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: The sequential agent enforces order through code structure.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: A loop repeats work and retrieves one source per iteration, violating [concurrent execution]. Independent lookups still yield results sequentially but take longer.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Parallel execution, distinct output keys, and subsequent merging satisfy concurrency and combination. The tradeoff is another merge agent and LLM call.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It preserves concurrency, but nondeterministic arrival order changes concatenated results across runs and omits a synthesis step, violating [combined output].
- **{{option:F}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Simultaneous execution prevents summarization, translation, and review from waiting for preceding outputs, violating [always this order].

Also note: Documentation indicates that from ADK 2.0, Python and Go template workflows are moving toward replacement by graph-based and dynamic workflows.

**References**: [Workflows (ADK)](https://adk.dev/workflows/) · [Parallel agents (ADK)](https://adk.dev/agents/workflow-agents/parallel-agents/)

questions.title: Fixing a LoopAgent that continues after reaching its target
questions.prompt:
An ADK document-improvement agent alternates writer and critic agents inside `LoopAgent`. The loop continues even after the critic says "no issues," wasting cost. Requirements:

- Stop **immediately** when critique passes.
- Stop after **at most four iterations** even if it never passes.
- **Retain** the existing `LoopAgent` and writer/critic structure.

Which change best fits?

options.text: Set only `max_iterations=4` on `LoopAgent`, leaving flow and termination signals unchanged.
Add a critic-side exit tool that sets `escalate` upon passing, without specifying `max_iterations`.
Add an exit tool that sets `escalate` upon passing, and also set `max_iterations=4`.
Remove `LoopAgent` and have application code call a writer/critic sequential agent up to four times, inspecting critique and stopping on success.

questions.explanation:
ADK documentation says `LoopAgent` does not decide when to stop by itself; an explicit stopping mechanism is required. Either `max_iterations` caps iterations or a subagent signals termination. In Python, the latter uses a tool setting `tool_context.actions.escalate = True`; the documented example has the improver call `exit_loop` when critique passes. The decisive requirements are [stop immediately on passing], [at most four], and [retain existing structure].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It stops at four but performs remaining iterations after passing, violating [stop immediately].
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It stops on passing but can continue indefinitely if critique never passes, violating [at most four].
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: The termination signal and iteration cap cover each other's gaps. The tradeoff is capped cases ending below standard and needing marking or separate handling.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Code can enforce both stopping conditions, but replacing `LoopAgent` with application iteration control violates [retain existing structure].

**References**: [Loop agents (ADK)](https://adk.dev/agents/workflow-agents/loop-agents/)

questions.title: Matching runaway controls to platform settings
questions.prompt:
Platforms name agent runaway controls differently. Match each control on the left to its platform setting on the right. One setting is unused.

| Number | Control |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Limit nesting depth when Claude Agent SDK subagents spawn further subagents. |
| 2 | Cap estimated spending for an entire Claude Agent SDK query, including subagents. |
| 3 | Raise `MaxTurnsExceeded` when an OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) agent loop exceeds its LLM-call count. |
| 4 | Limit concurrent OpenAI Agents API subagents, excluding the coordinator. |
| 5 | Provide an ADK `LoopAgent` iteration safety net if no termination signal occurs. |

| Symbol | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| a | `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` |
| b | `max_budget_usd` |
| c | `max_turns` |
| d | `max_concurrent_subagents` |
| e | `max_iterations` |
| f | `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` |

options.text: `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH`
`max_budget_usd`
`max_turns`
`max_concurrent_subagents`
`max_iterations`
`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`

items.text: Limit nesting depth when Claude Agent SDK subagents spawn further subagents.
Cap estimated spending for an entire Claude Agent SDK query, including subagents.
Raise `MaxTurnsExceeded` when an OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) agent loop exceeds its LLM-call count.
Limit concurrent OpenAI Agents API subagents, excluding the coordinator.
Provide an ADK `LoopAgent` iteration safety net if no termination signal occurs.

questions.explanation:
Runaway controls use different units across platforms. Agent SDK controls depth/concurrency through environment variables and spend through a query option. Agents SDK caps loop LLM calls with `max_turns`; Agents API caps concurrent subagents with `max_concurrent_subagents`; ADK caps `LoopAgent` iterations with `max_iterations`. Each row's platform and target—depth, spend, LLM calls, concurrency, or iterations—determine the match.

| Number | Answer | Decisive reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | {{option:a}} | `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` defaults to three levels; a value of 1 prevents subagents spawning their own subagents. |
| 2 | {{option:b}} | `max_budget_usd`, or TypeScript `maxBudgetUsd`, applies to whole-query spending including subagent requests and ends with `error_max_budget_usd` when reached. |
| 3 | {{option:c}} | Agents SDK raises `MaxTurnsExceeded` after `max_turns`; a turn here is an LLM call in the agent loop. |
| 4 | {{option:d}} | Agents API `max_concurrent_subagents` defaults to 6 and excludes the coordinator. |
| 5 | {{option:e}} | `LoopAgent` does not decide when to stop, so `max_iterations` supplies a safety net. |

{{option:f}}, `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`, is a real Agent SDK concurrency limit, defaulting to 20, but no row asks about Claude Agent SDK concurrency. Row 4 asks about OpenAI Agents API and must not be confused with {{option:f}}.

**References**: [Subagents in the SDK › Cap subagent depth, concurrency, and spend](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents) · [How the agent loop works › Turns and budget](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop) · [Running agents (OpenAI Agents SDK)](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/) · [Multi-agent (OpenAI Agents API)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/multi-agent) · [Loop agents (ADK)](https://adk.dev/agents/workflow-agents/loop-agents/)

questions.title: Delegation for a Managed Agents code-review coordinator
questions.prompt:
A PR code-review coordinator uses Claude Managed Agents beta. PRs change 5–400 files, with security, performance, and style reviewers assigned by file group. All agents in one session share a sandbox/filesystem; reviewers only read code. Requirements:

- The coordinator must send **follow-up questions** such as "explain the evidence behind this finding."
- Manage each PR under **one session budget**, configurable only at session creation.
- Process even 400-file PRs within one session while respecting **25 simultaneous child threads**, including idle threads.
- Avoid **accumulating consultation-call charges** for a higher-tier advisor model.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Have the coordinator directly review each file group while consulting a stronger advisor model, without reviewer subagents.
Delegate file groups to reviewer subagents, grouping files more broadly for large PRs to keep subagents within 25.
Have the coordinator dynamically create workflows with hundreds of per-file review agents running in parallel stages, then combine results.
Create a separate Managed Agents session per file group for parallel review and combine session outputs in application code.

questions.explanation:
Managed Agents multi-agent capabilities include subagent delegation, dynamic workflows, and advisors. Previously invoked subagents accept follow-up messages; workflow execution threads do not, and the server archives them after execution. Advisors provide stronger-model advice while the agent does the work itself; consultations are charged at advisor rates against the session budget. Sessions allow at most 25 simultaneous child threads, including idle ones, with one-level delegation depth. The decisive requirements are [follow-up questions], [one session budget], [25 child threads], and [avoid consultation charges].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: An advisor is not a subagent, so there are no parallel reviewers. Per-group consultations accumulate charges against the budget, violating [avoid consultation charges].
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Delegation supports follow-ups, keeps reviewers within one session/budget, and grouped files keep thread counts within limits. Tradeoffs are larger reviewer contexts and longer processing for large PRs, with parallelism capped at 25.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It favors large-scale parallelism, but workflow threads cannot receive follow-up questions.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Separate sessions avoid thread limits but split spending across budgets, violating [one session budget] and losing the shared-sandbox benefit.

Also note: All listed subagents must either pin the same `inference_geo` or all leave it unpinned; mismatch returns a 400 validation error. The feature requires beta header `managed-agents-2026-04-01`.

**References**: [Multiagent orchestration (Claude Managed Agents)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/multi-agent)

questions.title: Parallel competitor research and result delivery
questions.prompt:
A research team uses agents to compare three competitors' plans and features. Each competitor contributes a table with dozens of rows, requiring roughly a dozen web searches. Requirements:

- Table values **must not be summarized or altered** through the coordinator.
- Full subresearch outputs **must not accumulate in coordinator context**.
- Cost policy allows **at most five subagents** per report.
- Meet the **deadline**; sequential research of all three competitors by one agent would miss it.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Run one subagent per competitor, three in parallel, specifying objectives, output format, and scope; return full tables in messages for the coordinator to transcribe into its report.
Have one agent research competitors sequentially and save tables to files, then assemble the report with those files unchanged.

Run one subagent per competitor, three in parallel, specifying objectives, output format, and scope; save tables to files and return only references. The coordinator writes prose and inserts files unchanged.

Split each competitor into plans, features, reviews, and support, spawning 12 parallel subagents with objectives, format, and scope; save tables to files and return references for unchanged insertion.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's multi-agent research article says saving subagent results externally and returning lightweight references reduces information loss and token overhead from copying large outputs through conversation history. This suits structured outputs such as reports, code, and visualizations. It reports up to 90% lower research time for complex queries when a lead runs 3–5 parallel subagents that also parallelize tools; direct comparisons typically warrant 2–4 subagents. Incorrect options violate [unchanged table values], [coordinator context], [at most five subagents], or [deadline].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Parallelism meets deadline/count limits, but transmitting and transcribing full tables risks changed or omitted values and context accumulation, violating both data-preservation requirements.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, appropriate for a different situation)**: Files preserve values at minimal cost, but sequential research misses [deadline]. This suits smaller research without parallelism needs.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Three parallel subagents research while tables bypass coordinator rewriting through files, meeting all four constraints. There are three tradeoffs: higher token usage than one agent (the article reports agents at roughly 4× chat and multi-agent systems at 15×); inability to steer running subagents and waiting for the slowest; and maintaining external storage and output-format contracts.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: It minimizes time and uses correct delivery, but 12 subagents violate [at most five], exceed the direct-comparison guideline of 2–4, and increase token cost.

**References**: [How we built our multi-agent research system › Effort scaling, Parallelization, Synchronous bottleneck, Filesystem output](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)

questions.title: Choosing a compliance-review agent architecture
questions.prompt: Considering NuriComply's [Requirement 1], the six-hour window in [Requirement 2], and staffing in [Company overview], which architecture is most appropriate?
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** NuriComply operates a SaaS service checking corporate customer contracts against internal policies and statutory clauses. Staff previously selected documents and initiated reviews on request. Overnight review is now being automated with the Claude Agent SDK. **Two engineers** own this work.
>
> **[Requirement 1]** A request covers 40–600 contracts scattered across customer-repository folders. Contracts, addenda, and scanned notes are mixed together; content determines which documents belong in a review bundle. Bundle reviews are independent, followed by one report organized by violation type. Reviews are read-only, with no side effects such as sending messages or refunds.
>
> **[Requirement 2]** The overnight window is **six hours**, with a **$60 billing limit** per request. Unreviewed bundles within the budget/window are acceptable, but the report **must identify them**. Results from every completed bundle must appear.
>
> **[Operational settings]** Subagents have depth 1, so cannot spawn subagents, and concurrency 8. Each subagent response costs at most approximately $1.
>
> **[Other information]** Contract OCR will be replaced next quarter, and the team separately operates an internal-policy Q&A chatbot.

options.text: Have code fix the folder file list, run the same review call per file in parallel, and combine results in a fixed workflow.
Have one agent explore folders, determine bundles, review them sequentially, and synthesize the report in the same context.
Have a lead agent explore folders and determine bundles, delegate each bundle to a subagent, and synthesize their results into a report.
Use lead/subagents but attach a separate critic to each subagent, repeating reviews until they meet the standard.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's agent-design article recommends orchestrator-workers when subtasks cannot be predicted in advance and a central LLM must determine them from input, then synthesize worker results. Its multi-agent article highlights benefits for independent parallel directions and information exceeding one context window, at substantial token cost. Decisive evidence is [Requirement 1]'s content-dependent bundles and independent reviews, [Requirement 2]'s six-hour/$60 limits, and [Company overview]'s two engineers.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Fixed parallelization suits predefined subtasks. Content-dependent document types and bundles make per-file fixed review violate [Requirement 1]'s grouping need.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Simple architecture, but sequential review of up to 600 contracts within one context threatens the six-hour window and increases long-context omissions.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: The lead groups documents while subagents independently review in parallel, each with fresh context and returning summaries, addressing time and context constraints. The tradeoff is much higher token consumption and earlier arrival at the $60 cap, leaving some bundles unreviewed, which is explicitly allowed.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: Iterative critique may improve quality but multiplies calls, conflicting with the $60 budget and two-person operations. Evaluator-optimizer suits clear criteria and valuable iteration.

The OCR replacement and policy Q&A chatbot are distractors unrelated to this architecture.

**References**: [Building effective agents › Workflow: Orchestrator-workers](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [How we built our multi-agent research system › Token usage and when multi-agent fits](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) · [Effective context engineering for AI agents › Sub-agent architectures](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)

questions.title: Handling partial results when the spending cap is reached
questions.prompt: Implement Q34's architecture with `max_budget_usd`. Considering [Requirement 2]'s mandatory inclusion of completed bundles, identification of unreviewed bundles, and $60 limit, together with [Operational settings]'s concurrency of eight and approximately $1 maximum per response, how should partial results from a budget-limited overnight run be handled?
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** NuriComply operates a SaaS service checking corporate customer contracts against internal policies and statutory clauses. Staff previously selected documents and initiated reviews on request. Overnight review is now being automated with the Claude Agent SDK. **Two engineers** own this work.
>
> **[Requirement 1]** A request covers 40–600 contracts scattered across customer-repository folders. Contracts, addenda, and scanned notes are mixed together; content determines which documents belong in a review bundle. Bundle reviews are independent, followed by one report organized by violation type. Reviews are read-only, with no side effects such as sending messages or refunds.
>
> **[Requirement 2]** The overnight window is **six hours**, with a **$60 billing limit** per request. Unreviewed bundles within the budget/window are acceptable, but the report **must identify them**. Results from every completed bundle must appear.
>
> **[Operational settings]** Subagents have depth 1, so cannot spawn subagents, and concurrency 8. Each subagent response costs at most approximately $1.
>
> **[Other information]** Contract OCR will be replaced next quarter, and the team separately operates an internal-policy Q&A chatbot.

options.text: Save bundle results through a `SubagentStop` hook whenever a subagent finishes, set `max_budget_usd` to $50, and build the report from saved results and the unreviewed list after a budget error.
Set `max_budget_usd` to $50 and use the synthesized text in `ResultMessage.result` as the report, including after budget termination.
Give each subagent a low `maxTurns` to finish early, include partial-marked outputs unchanged in the report, and use a $50 budget.
Immediately resume the same session with a larger budget after reaching the cap, review every remaining bundle, and then produce the report.

questions.explanation:
Agent SDK budgets include subagent spending. At the cap, the SDK blocks new subagents, stops running background subagents, and ends with `error_max_budget_usd`, whose result has no `result` field. Checks occur after responses, permitting overshoot from the triggering response and already-running subagents. Start/stop hooks can collect parallel results. With eight concurrent subagents and approximately $1 per response, overshoot stays within about $10, making a $50 cap fit the $60 limit. Decisive requirements are [include completed results], [identify unreviewed bundles], and $60.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Persisting each completed result prevents loss at budget termination. Unreviewed bundles are the difference between the complete bundle list and saved results. Tradeoffs are stopping earlier with a below-limit cap and maintaining hooks/storage integration.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The cap fits, but budget termination has no `result` field, so synthesized text cannot be read, violating inclusion of completed bundles.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Subagents hitting `maxTurns` return partial-marked output. Including interrupted reviews conflicts with relying on fully reviewed bundles and merely reduces review coverage.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It reviews more bundles, but raising the budget and continuing exceeds the $60 billing limit.

The OCR replacement and policy Q&A chatbot are unrelated distractors.

**References**: [How the agent loop works › Budget headroom](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop) · [How the agent loop works › Handle the result](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop) · [Subagents in the SDK › Cap subagent depth, concurrency, and spend](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents) · [How the agent loop works › Hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop)

questions.title: Loading context for queries against stable regulations
questions.prompt:
Design context for a financial-regulation query agent. A roughly 5,000-token overview changes quarterly; thousands of provisions cross-reference one another, and each question needs different provisions. Requirements:

- Keep p95 latency **at its current level**.
- **Avoid context rot**, where long input destabilizes accuracy.
- Let the agent **follow and read cross-references**.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Put the entire overview and all provisions in the system prompt, using prompt caching to reduce latency.
Preload nothing, including the overview; let the agent find and read everything each time through file paths and search tools.
Preselect top provisions through embedding search for each question, append them to the prompt, and provide no tools for further reading.
Preload the overview, represent provisions by paths, and let the agent use search/read tools to find necessary content and follow references.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's context-engineering article describes lightweight identifiers such as file paths for runtime tool retrieval and a hybrid approach combining preloaded content with autonomous exploration. Runtime exploration is slower than retrieving precomputed data; poor tools or search heuristics can waste context. Hybrid loading suits relatively stable domains such as law and finance. The article also describes context rot: accurate recall declines as context grows. The decisive requirements are [retain p95], [avoid context rot], and [follow references].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Caching reduces latency, but loading thousands of provisions directly causes context rot.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Selective reading avoids rot and supports references, but repeatedly searching even the unchanged overview adds round trips, violating [retain p95].
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Preretrieval is fast and limits rot, but without reading tools the agent cannot follow referenced provisions.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Preloading the stable overview reduces round trips; selective provision reading avoids rot and supports references. The tradeoff is dependence on search-tool and path-structure quality.

**References**: [Effective context engineering for AI agents › Context retrieval and agentic search](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents) · [Effective context engineering for AI agents › Context rot](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)

questions.title: Long-context strategy for six-hour unattended codebase research
questions.prompt:
A Claude API team builds an agent to investigate dependencies across a 40-module legacy codebase unattended for up to six hours. Each module requires reading hundreds of files; investigations are independent. The current single agent increasingly forgets earlier content while token cost grows. Requirements:

- Final reporting must preserve module conclusions and **exact supporting code locations**.
- Finish within six hours; sequential module work would exceed the window.
- Total token cost must stay **within twice** the current single-agent run.
- There are **two operations engineers**.

Which strategy best fits?

options.text: Keep one agent with threshold compaction, instructing summaries to retain every module conclusion and code location before continuing.
Run module subagents in parallel, receiving 1,000–2,000-token summaries with conclusions and code locations; have the lead record these in a notes file and write the report.
Run module subagents in parallel but return all file contents and intermediate reasoning to the lead for full review before reporting.
Keep one agent with old-tool-result clearing and record conclusions/code locations in a notes file after each module.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's context-engineering article distinguishes three long-task techniques: compaction for interaction-heavy work, structured notes for iterative work with clear milestones, and subagents for complex research benefiting from parallel exploration. Subagents may consume tens of thousands of tokens while returning only 1,000–2,000-token summaries, keeping lead context focused. Independent, read-heavy module research with a deadline fits subagents; notes preserve conclusions and exact locations. The decisive requirements are [exact code locations], [six hours], and [within 2× cost].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Cost is low, but summaries can lose code-location details, violating exactness, and sequential work also exceeds the window.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Parallel subagents meet the window, fresh contexts and concise summaries limit rot/cost, and notes preserve conclusions/locations. Tradeoffs are summary information loss, higher total tokens, and orchestration complexity, accepted within the stated limits.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: Parallelism addresses time, but returning every source balloons lead context, violates [within 2× cost], and eliminates subagent benefits.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It manages cost and accuracy, but sequential work exceeds six hours. Clearing old results does not shorten sequential execution.

questions.title: Safeguards for a file-based agent memory handler
questions.prompt:
A team builds long-term memory as a client-side tool: the model requests file reads/writes with paths, and the application executes them against team-owned object storage. The handler must ensure:

- Model-requested paths **cannot reach files outside the memory root**.
- Memory files **cannot grow indefinitely**, and stale files do not accumulate.

Choose **two** safeguards meeting these requirements.

options.text: Remove the literal `../` from requested paths and concatenate them directly onto the storage path.
Use separate directories per user, but skip path validation and assume the model stays within its instructed directory.
Check the memory prefix on every path, canonicalize it, verify it remains inside the memory root, and reject paths outside.
Instruct the system prompt never to request paths outside the memory directory, while executing received paths without validation.
Cap file size and characters returned by `view`, and periodically delete files not accessed for a long time.
Tell the model to clean old content when memory grows, without handler-enforced size or retention limits.

questions.explanation:
Claude's memory-tool documentation says it runs client-side and the application executes every file operation, so security is the application's responsibility. Validate prefixes and canonicalize paths before checking root containment, accounting for `../`, backslash variants such as `..\`, URL-encoded variants, and other bypasses. It also recommends file-size limits, `view` character limits, and periodic deletion of long-unused files. The decisive requirements are [block access outside root] and [prevent unlimited growth/stale files].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Literal removal can miss encoded variants or nested patterns and cannot replace canonicalization plus root checks.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Per-user directories help, but unvalidated model paths do not enforce containment. Isolation and path validation are different safeguards.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Prefix checking, canonicalization, and root containment are the documented validation sequence.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The model can disobey or be manipulated, so instructions cannot guarantee containment; handler code must enforce it.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: Size caps, output limits, and expiration cleanup are documented capacity controls.
- **{{option:F}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Model-managed cleanup does not enforce bounded growth or stale-file removal. Files keep growing if cleanup is omitted.

Also note: Documentation says Claude generally refuses to write sensitive information to memory, but stronger guarantees require handler-side validation removing sensitive data before writes.

**References**: [Memory tool › Security considerations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool)

questions.title: Combining tenant-specific memory and context editing in SaaS
questions.prompt:
A Claude API SaaS team runs contract-review agents per customer organization. Agents read contracts with `read_contract` and later cite exact values such as contract-condition tables. Long sessions need old-result clearing with `clear_tool_uses_20250919`, alongside `memory_20250818`. Requirements:

- Customer memories **must not mix**, for audit compliance.
- **Exact condition values must survive** clearing.
- Continue reducing input tokens; **do not abandon tool-result clearing**.
- Introduce **no new storage infrastructure** beyond existing object storage this quarter.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Keep all customer memory in one shared storage path, distinguishing filenames by customer ID, and prompt preservation of exact values near the clearing threshold.
Omit memory and add `read_contract` to `exclude_tools`, clearing only other tool results.
Map memory paths to customer-specific object-storage prefixes in the handler, enable clearing, and have the agent preserve exact values in memory when warned near the threshold.
Use only threshold compaction without tool-result clearing, instruct summaries to transcribe exact values, and omit memory.

questions.explanation:
Memory is client-side: applications choose storage and map virtual paths to actual locations such as user directories or database keys. Combined with context editing, Claude automatically receives a preservation warning near the clearing threshold and can save tool results to memory before deletion. `exclude_tools` can exempt tools, but their results and tokens remain. The decisive requirements are [tenant memory isolation], [exact-value preservation], [retain clearing], and [no new infrastructure].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Clearing and storage work, but filename distinctions in one shared namespace do not structurally enforce tenant isolation in the handler.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It preserves exact values without new infrastructure, but contract-result tokens remain, violating the required clearing approach.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Handler mapping provides isolation, warning-triggered memory writes preserve values, and clearing reduces tokens. Tradeoffs are the model potentially missing a save, application-owned mapping/access controls, and extra output tokens/tool calls for storage.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: No new infrastructure is needed, but model-written summaries can alter exact table values, and it abandons required tool-result clearing. Exact preservation is not guaranteed.

Also note: Context editing requires beta header `context-management-2025-06-27`.

questions.title: Handling model-specific defaults for thinking cleanup
questions.prompt:
One Claude API agent codebase calls both Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5. Both use thinking and the same context-editing beta `edits` configuration. Requirements:

- **Retain previous-turn thinking identically for both models** to preserve cache hits.
- When input grows, clear old tool results only when at least **50,000 tokens** can be removed, justifying cache-write costs.
- Use one configuration without code branches.

Which `edits` configuration best fits?

options.text: First explicitly set `clear_thinking_20251015` with `keep: "all"`, then `clear_tool_uses_20250919` with `clear_at_least` of 50,000 tokens.
First add `clear_thinking_20251015` without `keep`, then `clear_tool_uses_20250919` with `clear_at_least` of 50,000 tokens.
First set `clear_thinking_20251015` with `keep` specifying `thinking_turns` of 2, then `clear_tool_uses_20250919` with `clear_at_least` of 50,000 tokens.
First explicitly set `clear_thinking_20251015` with `keep: "all"`, but omit tool-result clearing.

questions.explanation:
Documentation says `clear_thinking_20251015` defaults for `keep` vary: models including Opus 4.5 and later retain all turns, while earlier models and Haiku through 4.5 retain only the last turn. Code spanning model tiers should specify `keep` rather than rely on defaults. Keeping thinking preserves prompt cache; clearing invalidates it from the removal point. Tool-result `clear_at_least` sets a minimum removal amount to offset cache-write cost. When combining strategies, thinking cleanup comes first in `edits`. The decisive requirements are [identical retention across models] and [at least 50,000 tokens cleared].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Explicit `keep` aligns model behavior, with minimum-volume tool clearing. The tradeoff is accumulated thinking making input larger than alternatives, partly relieved by tool clearing.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Tool clearing is correct, but omitted `keep` invokes model defaults; Haiku 4.5 retains only the last turn, violating identical retention.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Behavior matches across models, but removing older thinking invalidates cache from that point, violating cache preservation.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Thinking retention matches, but omitting tool clearing prevents input reduction and violates [clear old tool results when input grows].

questions.title: Null compaction content in an agent with tool definitions
questions.prompt:
A Claude API agent uses threshold compaction (`compact_20260112`, beta). With several tools defined, some compaction responses have a `compaction` block whose `content` is `null`. Requirements:

- Summaries must contain **progress, remaining work, and settled decisions**.
- **Retain identical tool definitions** on every request to preserve the cache prefix.
- Resolve this **within the same request flow**, without human intervention.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Lower `trigger` so compaction occurs earlier with smaller context.
Enable `pause_after_compaction`, then ignore empty blocks and continue using only recent messages.
Omit tool definitions only on compaction requests to prevent tool calls during summarization.
Use `instructions` to require text-only summarization without tool calls, explicitly listing progress, remaining work, and decisions.

questions.explanation:
Compaction documentation says that with tools defined, the model may attempt a tool call instead of summarizing during the internal summary stage, producing a compaction block with `content: null`. It recommends `instructions` prohibiting tool calls and requiring text-only output. These instructions replace the default summarization prompt entirely rather than supplement it, so required content must also be specified. The decisive requirements are [summary content], [retain tool definitions], and [same request flow].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, appropriate for a different situation)**: Earlier, more frequent compaction leaves the attempted-tool-call cause unchanged, so empty blocks may persist.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Flow continues, but discarding empty blocks leaves no summary and loses earlier progress, remaining work, and settled decisions.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It prevents tool calls during summarization but changes definitions across requests, breaking the cache prefix and violating [retain tool definitions].
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It prohibits the cause and specifies summary content, satisfying all requirements. The tradeoff is owning summary-instruction quality instead of using the default prompt.

questions.title: Server-side compaction and standalone compact calls under ZDR
questions.prompt:
An organization uses OpenAI Responses API with `store=false` on every request for Zero Data Retention, while the application holds the complete input array. It has two agents:

- **Customer conversation agent**: Users wait for responses. Compaction must happen **automatically within requests**, without a separate application call, while reducing request size and tail latency.
- **Overnight settlement agent**: Do not compact while processing a counterparty; the application must choose compaction timing **only at boundaries between counterparties**.

Choose **two** appropriate operating approaches.

options.text: Have the conversation agent call standalone `/responses/compact` after every turn, then use the reduced window for the next request.
Have the settlement agent set a low `compact_threshold`, triggering automatic server-side compaction as soon as input grows.
Enable server-side compaction for the conversation agent but retain every old item before the compaction item in subsequent input arrays.
Set `compact_threshold` for the conversation agent, append output items including compaction, and remove input items before the latest compaction item.
Have the settlement application call standalone `/responses/compact` between counterparties and use the returned window unchanged as its next input.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's compaction guide describes two modes. Server-side compaction uses request `compact_threshold` to compact automatically after the token threshold without a separate call, including with `store=false`. Stateless standalone `/responses/compact` gives direct timing control: send the full window and receive a compacted window; it is also ZDR-compatible. Compaction items are opaque rather than human-readable. For input-array chaining, deleting items before the latest compaction item reduces request size and tail latency; a standalone `/responses/compact` window should instead be passed unchanged, without pruning. The decisive requirements are [automatic within requests], [request size/tail latency], and [application chooses boundary timing].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It fits ZDR and reduces the window, but extra calls each turn violate [automatic within requests] and add user waiting time.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: A low threshold can compact mid-counterparty, violating boundary-only timing.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Compaction is automatic, but retaining old items grows request arrays and defeats size/tail-latency reduction.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Server-side compaction works with `store=false`; the application removes old items to reduce arrays. Tradeoffs are application array management and opaque state being difficult for humans to inspect.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: Application-controlled boundaries and unchanged returned windows preserve timing control and ZDR. The tradeoff is one extra call at each boundary.

**References**: [Compaction (OpenAI API guide)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction)

questions.title: Reducing delayed stream closure in a store=False compaction session
questions.prompt:
A voice-support service using OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) compresses history with `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` and `ModelSettings(store=False)`. It must transition promptly after the user finishes speaking, but long-history sessions leave streams open for seconds after the final token, delaying turn transitions. Requirements:

- **Retain history compaction** for long sessions so earlier state carries forward.
- **Keep `store=False`**.
- Reduce turn-transition latency.

What is the best action?

options.text: Fix `compaction_mode` to `"input"` so compact requests are reconstructed from current session items.
Disable automatic compaction and explicitly call `run_compaction()` in gaps before the user starts the next turn.
Use `SessionSettings(limit=...)` to load only recent items and stop using the compaction session.
Relax trigger conditions to reduce automatic compaction frequency.

questions.explanation:
`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` automatically compacts after qualifying turns. The SDK waits for compaction before `Runner.run(...)` returns or stream-event iteration ends, so expensive compaction can keep a stream open for seconds after its final token. Documentation recommends disabling automatic compaction and calling `run_compaction()` between turns for low-latency turn-taking. In `auto` mode, `store=False` already falls back to input-based compaction because the last response was not stored. The decisive requirements are [retain compaction], [retain store=False], and [reduce transition latency].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: `auto` already falls back to input mode with `store=False`, so behavior is unchanged. Compaction still runs before completion and transition latency remains.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Moving compaction off the response path reduces waiting while retaining compaction and `store=False`. Tradeoffs are application scheduling and potential overlap with the next turn if the gap is short.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It shortens input but merely omits old history without carrying state through a compaction item, violating [retain compaction].
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Frequency decreases, but turns that compact still close streams late, leaving their transition-latency problem unresolved.

**References**: [Sessions (OpenAI Agents SDK) › OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sessions/)

questions.title: Retaining all stored history while sending only the latest ten items
questions.prompt:
A customer-support service built with OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) uses session objects to persist conversation history. Growing history requires cost reduction. Requirements:

- **Continue using sessions** for storage and resumption.
- **Do not delete or modify stored history**, for audit purposes.
- Limit model input to **the latest ten items**.
- Restrict changes to execution settings, `RunConfig`.

Which method best fits?

options.text: Instruct the model to consult only the latest ten items while continuing to send all session history.
Stop using sessions and have the application slice the latest ten stored items into each call's input list.
Set `SessionSettings(limit=10)` in `RunConfig.session_settings`.
Wrap session storage to delete oldest items whenever its count exceeds ten.

questions.explanation:
Agents SDK `SessionSettings` controls how many session items are loaded: default `limit=None` loads all, while `limit=N` loads the most recent N. It can be set per run via `RunConfig.session_settings`; non-None values override session defaults. Sessions store only new-turn items, so persisted history remains intact. Sessions also cannot be combined in one run with server-managed continuation such as `conversation_id` or `previous_response_id`. The decisive requirements are [continue sessions], [preserve stored history], [latest ten], and [RunConfig only].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Minimal code change, but all history still incurs tokens and compliance depends on the model, violating the ten-item input limit.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It precisely limits input but abandons sessions and changes call code, violating two requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It limits loading without changing storage, meeting all four. The tradeoff is the model cannot see older context; other means are needed when that information matters.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It limits input by deleting stored records, violating history preservation.

**References**: [Sessions (OpenAI Agents SDK) › Session settings](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sessions/) · [Running agents (OpenAI Agents SDK) › Conversation management](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/)

questions.title: Sequence around automatic compaction in Agent SDK
questions.prompt:
A Claude Agent SDK team is designing the flow as a long-running agent approaches its context limit. Archive the full transcript before compaction removes it, and record compaction timing in the application. Arrange steps so **each step's result enables the next**.

- (1) The SDK emits a `compact_boundary` system message, and the application records compaction timing.
- (2) Accumulated conversation approaches the context-window limit.
- (3) A `PreCompact` hook archives the full pre-compaction transcript.
- (4) The SDK replaces older conversation history with a summary.

items.text: The SDK emits a `compact_boundary` system message, and the application records compaction timing.
Accumulated conversation approaches the context-window limit.
A `PreCompact` hook archives the full pre-compaction transcript.
The SDK replaces older conversation history with a summary.

questions.explanation:
Agent SDK documentation says approaching the context limit triggers summarization of old history, followed by a message with `type: "system"` and `subtype: "compact_boundary"`. `PreCompact` runs before compaction and can archive the full transcript. The ordering follows dependencies between steps.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (2) Context approaches limit | Starting point. | Automatic compaction begins near the window limit. |
| 2 | (3) Archive with `PreCompact` | Imminent compaction triggers the hook; archive before originals become a summary. | The hook runs immediately before compaction. |
| 3 | (4) Replace old history with summary | Archiving must finish before losing originals is safe. | Compaction replaces old history with a summary. |
| 4 | (1) Receive `compact_boundary` and record timing | The boundary message requires completed compaction. | This message occurs afterward. |

Also note: Compaction may fail to preserve initial-prompt instructions. Put persistent rules in `CLAUDE.md`, which is reinjected on each request.

**References**: [How the agent loop works › Automatic compaction](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop) · [How the agent loop works › Hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop)

questions.title: ADK state prefixes and persistence
questions.prompt:
An ADK (Python) support-agent team summarizes state-prefix scope and session-service persistence. Mark each statement Yes or No.

| Number | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | A `user:` value stored through `DatabaseSessionService` is readable in the same user's other sessions within the same app. |
| 2 | Because `app:` values are shared by all app users and sessions, they survive application restarts even with `InMemorySessionService`. |
| 3 | `temp:` values are discarded when the current invocation ends but are shared with subagent calls within it. |
| 4 | Writing `tool_context.state` inside a tool function is a recommended way to update session state. |

items.text: A `user:` value stored through `DatabaseSessionService` is readable in the same user's other sessions within the same app.
Because `app:` values are shared by all app users and sessions, they survive application restarts even with `InMemorySessionService`.
`temp:` values are discarded when the current invocation ends but are shared with subagent calls within it.
Writing `tool_context.state` inside a tool function is a recommended way to update session state.

questions.explanation:
ADK prefixes determine scope; session services determine persistence. Unprefixed values belong to the current session, `user:` spans the same user's sessions within an app, `app:` spans all app users/sessions, and `temp:` belongs only to the current invocation. Database and Vertex AI services persist non-`temp:` values, while in-memory services lose everything on restart. Statement 2 confuses sharing scope with persistence.

| Number | Verdict | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Yes | `user:` spans the user's sessions, and the database service persists it. |
| 2 | No | `app:` has broad sharing scope but disappears on restart with `InMemorySessionService`; broad scope does not imply persistence. |
| 3 | Yes | `temp:` exists only in the current invocation chain, including subagent calls, and is never persisted by a service. |
| 4 | Yes | Documentation recommends `output_key`, events containing `state_delta`, and callback/tool context `state` writes. Avoid directly modifying session objects fetched outside an invocation. |

Also note: Directly modifying `session.state` outside an invocation bypasses event history and may not persist in database or Vertex AI services.
