questions.title: Token-triggered event compaction and summarizer model selection
questions.prompt:
A long-running ADK (Python) support agent will enable event compaction through `App.EventsCompactionConfig`. Requirements:

- Trigger when **token usage reaches a threshold**, not after an event count.
- Preserve the latest **six events verbatim**, without summarizing them.
- Use a **dedicated summarization model**, not the main agent model.

Choose **two** settings that together satisfy all three.

options.text: Configure sliding-window compaction with `compaction_interval=5` and `overlap_size=1`.
Set `token_threshold` and `event_retention_size=6`.
Combine token settings (`token_threshold`, `event_retention_size=6`) with sliding-window `compaction_interval=20`.
Create `LlmEventSummarizer` with the dedicated model and pass it as the compaction summarizer.
Do not specify a dedicated model; only shorten summaries by editing `prompt_template`.

questions.explanation:
ADK supports two event-compaction modes. Token-based compaction triggers through `token_threshold` and retains `event_retention_size` recent events verbatim. Sliding windows compact every `compaction_interval` and include `overlap_size` earlier events again in the next summary. A summarizer object specifies the model. The requirements distinguish token timing, six verbatim events, and a dedicated model.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Event-count intervals violate token-based timing; overlap includes prior events in summaries rather than preserving recent events verbatim.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Token triggering plus recent-event retention satisfies the first two requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Token mode works, but with both configured it takes precedence only on turns exceeding the threshold. Otherwise, 20-event sliding-window compaction can still occur, violating token-only timing.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: The summarizer selects the model, satisfying requirement three; combined with {{option:B}}, all requirements are met.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Templates change summary instructions, not the model performing summarization.

Also note: Documentation does not separately specify defaults, so explicitly choose thresholds and retention counts for the service's context limits and costs.

questions.title: User-specific long-term memory with separate write paths and permissions
questions.prompt:
An insurance-support team will store user preferences in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Memory Bank. Requirements:

- Extract preferences after sessions, **without making the user response path wait**.
- Explicit "remember this" items must be saved **exactly as chosen by the agent**, without extraction-model rewriting.
- A separate recommendation service must **read only**, never modify memory.
- Different users' memories must not mix.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Call only background `GenerateMemories` after sessions, sending explicit items through extraction too; grant writers `memoryEditor`.
Give the agent `CreateMemory`, wait for every preference write before responding, and omit post-session generation; grant writers `memoryEditor`.
Extract general preferences with background `GenerateMemories` after sessions, use `CreateMemory` for explicit items, grant writers `memoryEditor`, and grant recommendations `memoryViewer`.
Use both `GenerateMemories` and `CreateMemory`, but simplify operations by granting every service account, including recommendations, `memoryEditor`.

questions.explanation:
Memory Bank `GenerateMemories` uses an LLM to extract facts from conversation history and consolidate them with existing memory; background execution avoids agent waiting. `CreateMemory` lets the agent directly determine timing/content. Scopes, such as agent name and user, isolate consolidation and retrieval. IAM distinguishes read-only `memoryViewer` from creation/writing `memoryEditor`. The first three requirements distinguish the answers; all options share user-scope separation.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Background extraction and permissions fit, but routing explicit items through extraction violates preserving agent-chosen content; direct writing belongs to `CreateMemory`.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Direct writing preserves content, but waiting before responses violates the first requirement. Omitting automatic extraction also misses implicit preferences.

questions.title: Reducing selection errors among overlapping lookup tools
questions.prompt:
An internal support agent uses 60 tools on a shared MCP server and increasingly chooses the wrong tool. Analysis and constraints:

- Most errors confuse **overlapping lookup functions**, such as `lookup_customer_by_email`, `find_customer_by_phone`, and `get_account_summary`.
- Tool-definition tokens occupy only part of context and are not the problem.
- Most customer lookups require the same **three consecutive calls**, whose round trips exceed p95 latency budget.
- Four other agents use the server, so **existing server tools cannot be deleted or renamed**.
- Result tokens per customer lookup must be **less than the current three-call total**.

Which action best fits this agent?

options.text: Add `get_customer_context` combining consecutive lookups, expose it only to this agent and remove old tools from its exposure list. Return identity/status summaries by default, with detail controlled by a response-format argument.
Add `get_customer_context`, expose it only to this agent and hide old tools from this agent, but return all fields from all three tools without a response-format argument.
Add service/resource prefixes such as `crm_` and `billing_` and improve descriptions with boundaries/examples, retaining tool count and call sequence.
Delete the less-used overlapping tool from the server, extend the remaining tool's arguments for both purposes, and notify other agent teams.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's tool-design article recommends consolidating tools always called in the same sequence, with examples such as `schedule_event` and `get_customer_context`; overlapping purposes and excessive tool counts confuse agents. Response-format arguments or filtering manage oversized combined responses. The decisive requirements are [overlap confusion], [three-call latency], [no server-tool deletion], and [fewer result tokens].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It removes overlap, reduces three round trips to one, limits default output to a summary, and preserves existing server tools. Tradeoffs are an occasional additional detail call specifying format and one more combined tool to maintain.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It fixes overlap and round trips, but returning all fields produces at least the current total in context, violating fewer-result-tokens requirements.

- Reduce **model round trips per tool call**.

- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Code processes results without filling context and constructs each aggregation dynamically, avoiding predefinition. questions.title: Tool-search settings that preserve caching and direct access

A Claude Messages API team wants to reduce approximately 400 tool definitions with tool search and `defer_loading`. Requirements:

Deferred tools cannot carry `cache_control`; put breakpoints on nondeferred tools. Documentation recommends keeping the most-used 3–5 tools nondeferred. Direct access and cache-prefix/breakpoint requirements are decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Frequent tools remain directly callable while deferral reduces other definition tokens.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It reduces tokens but changes `tools` per request, disrupting prefix caching.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: A nondeferred breakpoint preserves the prefix despite deferred-tool discovery.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Nondeferred search works, but frequent tools also require discovery, violating direct access.

questions.title: Connecting a changing remote MCP server and a local server

A Claude Messages API purchasing agent will connect two MCP servers: a partner's remote HTTPS server that frequently adds tools and changes descriptions, and an internal local stdio file-search server. Requirements:

- Use **only approved partner tools**, never automatically adopting later additions.
- Keep partner tool definitions **identical throughout one conversation**.
- **Do not implement partner connection/reconnection in the application**.

Which configuration best fits?

Connect both through SDK MCP helpers, filter approved partner tools in application code, and manage connections there.

Use the MCP connector with default-disabled approved-tool `configs`, omit pinning, and connect the local server through SDK MCP helpers.

Additional beta header `mcp-client-2026-09-15` enables tool-list pinning so server changes do not affect Claude during a conversation. Use SDK MCP helpers for local servers or prompts/resources. Approved tools, fixed definitions, and no application-owned partner connection are decisive.

- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Filtering and local access work, but application client code owns partner connections, violating requirement three.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Allowlists satisfy approval, pinning fixes definitions, the connector manages remote connections, and helpers support local access. Tradeoffs are two connection approaches and dependence on two beta headers.

- Pass the current tenant ID in MCP `_meta` each call, **outside model control**.

Enable caching/invalidation and statically filter `delete_record`, but instruct the model to pass tenant ID as a tool argument.

Static filtering with `create_static_tool_filter` applies allowlists before denylists. `tool_meta_resolver` executes just before each call and sends run-context values in `_meta`. Invisible tools, model-independent metadata, and no server modifications distinguish the answers.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: SDK configuration meets these requirements without touching server code. The tradeoff is maintaining a procedure to detect definition changes and invalidate caches.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Vendor removal relies on changing unavailable server code, and uncached listing also violates requirement one.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Instructions prohibit use but leave the tool visible; instructions are not enforcement.

questions.title: Connecting tools through MCP and external agents through A2A
questions.prompt:
An ADK team building the NuriRepair mechanic application must integrate:

- A diagnostic scanner and repair-manual database: internal functions with structured inputs/outputs.
- A parts supplier's order-negotiation agent: operated by another organization, exchanging inventory questions, substitute proposals, and price negotiations over multiple turns; order confirmation may take hours.

Requirements:

- Support **multi-turn negotiation**.
- While waiting, the mechanic app cannot maintain a connection or poll, but must receive confirmation **within one minute**.
- **Do not add agent services** for the scanner/manual database.
- Security permits one authenticated external HTTPS receiver.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Use MCP for scanner/manual tools and A2A for the supplier; keep an SSE connection open for order-completion events, following Agent Card authentication.
Wrap everything as MCP tools, implementing negotiation calls and storing state in the application database, with the supplier API key in headers.
Use MCP tools and A2A, polling order-task status every 90 seconds before notifying the app, following Agent Card authentication.
Use MCP tools and A2A, receive the supplier's completion push notification and forward it to the app, following Agent Card authentication.

Multi-turn negotiation, no persistent connection/polling with one-minute notification, and no extra tool-agent services determine the choice.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Tool/agent separation fits, but waiting through SSE requires a persistent connection, violating requirement two.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It avoids extra services, but wrapping stateful multi-turn negotiation as stateless tool calls loses negotiation context/task state and violates requirement one.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Task tracking works, but polling is prohibited and 90-second intervals exceed the one-minute notification target.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: A2A tasks handle negotiation, MCP handles functions, and push notifications provide prompt updates without a retained connection. The tradeoff is owning receiver authentication and notification handling.

questions.title: Returning results when one computer-use action fails
questions.prompt:
A Claude API computer-use loop uses `computer_toolset_20260801`. One response contains four `tool_use` blocks in order: `left_click`, `type`, `key`, `screenshot`. The second action, `type`, fails. Requirements:

- Actions **depend on predecessors**, so execute sequentially and stop after failure.
- Let the model distinguish **success, failure, and nonexecution** and replan next turn.
- Leave no `tool_use` block unanswered.

Choose **two** appropriate result-handling actions.

options.text: Execute all four in parallel and return `tool_result` in completion order, including failed actions.
Mark failed `type` with `is_error`, but continue executing `key` and `screenshot` and return normal results.
Return `tool_result` for failed `type` with `is_error: true` and an error explanation.
Return successful `OK` for `left_click`, failed `type`, and both remaining blocks, appending a current screenshot.
Return `tool_result` with `is_error: true` for remaining `key`/`screenshot`, explaining they were not executed because the preceding action failed.

questions.explanation:
The computer-use loop must execute multiple actions sequentially and return one `tool_result` for every `tool_use`; unanswered blocks cause `invalid_request_error`. On failure, stop the rest of the batch, return `is_error: true` with a reason for the failed block, and error-marked nonexecution results for later blocks. This lets the model distinguish success/failure/skipping and replan. Each result needs `toolset_name: "computer"`. Sequential dependencies and distinguishable states are decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: All blocks receive results, but parallelism breaks dependencies, such as typing into the focus established by the click.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Continuing after failure can execute keys against an unexpected screen state, violating stop-after-failure.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It communicates the failed action and reason for replanning.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Formatting is complete, but success claims for failures/skips mislead the model. One screenshot cannot replace explicit distinctions.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: Explicit nonexecution results satisfy both stopping and complete response coverage.

questions.title: Connecting a payment agent with structured inputs
questions.prompt: Which connection design best satisfies all of Hanbada Travel's [Requirement 1]?
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** Hanbada Travel provides flight and accommodation booking assistance. It has eight engineers; its support agent uses OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) and a Responses API model from gpt-5.4 onward.
>
> **[Existing environment]** One support agent has approximately 40 function tools for flights, accommodation, profiles, mileage, and itinerary guidance; most turns use only three or four. Two local MCP servers provide fares, whose definitions change roughly quarterly, and customers, whose schemas change several times daily. A separate payment agent handles payments. Customers enter card details directly on a separate payment screen, never in agent conversations. An internal-messenger notification tool is outside this redesign's scope.
>

Send only order ID, amount, and currency to the payment agent **as structured data**, never full conversation history or notes containing personal information. Payment execution requires **support-manager approval**.
>
> **[Requirement 2]** Initially expose **fewer than 20 function tools**. The customer server's `delete_customer` must be **invisible** to the support agent. Avoid repeated fare-server `list_tools()` latency, but **never use stale customer schemas**.

options.text: Handoff to payment with `input_filter` removing notes/personal information from history, then handoff back after payment.
Expose payment through `as_tool`, set `parameters` to a Pydantic model containing only order ID/amount/currency, and enable `needs_approval` for manager approval before execution.
Expose payment through `as_tool`, pass the same `session` as support so it can find needed context, and enable `needs_approval`.
Expose payment through `as_tool` using default `{"input": "..."}` prose for order information, and enable `needs_approval`.

Handoffs transfer conversation control, with recipient history governed by filters. `Agent.as_tool` keeps control with support while calling another agent as a tool; `parameters` supports structured Pydantic/dataclass inputs, and nested runs do not inherit parent conversation state. `needs_approval` applies to `as_tool`, pausing before execution. The decisive requirements are continued support control, structured input, and approval-only execution.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Filtering can reduce personal data and handoff back is possible, but transferring control violates continuous support ownership; approval needs separate configuration.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It retains control, limits input fields through a model, and requires approval. Tradeoffs are potentially incorrect model-filled values, requiring approval checks, and approval waiting time.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Control and approval fit, but sharing the session exposes full history and notes, violating data restriction.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Control and approval fit, but free-form prose does not constrain fields and may mix in other context, violating structured input.

questions.title: Tool exposure, deferred loading, MCP caching, and filtering
questions.prompt: Considering Hanbada Travel's [Requirement 2] and [Existing environment], which configuration is most appropriate?
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** Hanbada Travel provides flight and accommodation booking assistance. It has eight engineers; its support agent uses OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) and a Responses API model from gpt-5.4 onward.
>
> **[Existing environment]** One support agent has approximately 40 function tools for flights, accommodation, profiles, mileage, and itinerary guidance; most turns use only three or four. Two local MCP servers provide fares, whose definitions change roughly quarterly, and customers, whose schemas change several times daily. A separate payment agent handles payments. Customers enter card details directly on a separate payment screen, never in agent conversations. An internal-messenger notification tool is outside this redesign's scope.
>
> **[Requirement 1]** The **support agent retains the customer conversation throughout**, including itinerary guidance after payment. Send only order ID, amount, and currency to the payment agent **as structured data**, never full conversation history or notes containing personal information. Payment execution requires **support-manager approval**.
>
> **[Requirement 2]** Initially expose **fewer than 20 function tools**. The customer server's `delete_customer` must be **invisible** to the support agent. Avoid repeated fare-server `list_tools()` latency, but **never use stale customer schemas**.

options.text: Enable `cache_tools_list` on both MCP servers, statically exclude `delete_customer`, expose only a few frequent functions immediately, defer others through domain namespaces, and add `ToolSearchTool`.
Cache only fares and statically exclude `delete_customer`, but immediately expose all approximately 40 functions with improved descriptions.
Cache only fares, statically exclude `delete_customer`, expose a few frequent functions immediately, defer others through domain namespaces, and add `ToolSearchTool`.
Cache only fares, prohibit `delete_customer` in instructions, expose a few frequent functions immediately, defer others through domain namespaces, and add `ToolSearchTool`.

questions.explanation:
Enable MCP `cache_tools_list` only when definitions rarely change. Static filters remove specified tools from model exposure. Tool search covers deferred functions/namespaces, with one `ToolSearchTool` per agent. OpenAI recommends fewer than 20 initially exposed functions. The decisive requirements are fewer than 20, invisible deletion, and no stale schemas.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Exposure and filtering fit, but caching customer schemas that change several times daily risks stale definitions.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Cache scope and filtering fit, but exposing approximately 40 functions violates the count limit.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Cache rarely changing fares only, hide the risky tool through filtering, and reduce initial exposure through deferral. Tradeoffs are customer-list retrieval latency every run and an extra search round trip when deferred tools are needed.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Instructions do not hide `delete_customer`, so it remains visible despite proper caching/count.

Also note: Local MCP tools are not among tool search's deferred targets—functions, namespaces, and hosted MCP—so deferral here applies only to function tools.

questions.title: A PreToolUse hook blocking only deletion in unattended runs
questions.prompt:
An unattended nightly Claude Code agent, v2.1.295 or later, has an allow rule for all `Bash`. The team wants to block deletion through `rm`, `unlink`, and `find … -delete`. Requirements:

- **Always block deletion**, without relying on approval prompts.
- Other Bash commands continue **without confirmation**.
- Deletion must remain blocked if the check exits 1, times out, or fails to start.
- Check-script failures must not block unrelated commands such as `npm test` and **stop nightly work**.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Keep Bash allow; create separate PreToolUse command-hook handlers with `if` filters for `rm *`, `unlink *`, and `find *`, exiting 2 for deletion patterns and setting `"onFailure": "block"` on each.
Keep Bash allow; run one PreToolUse command hook on every Bash call, exiting 2 for deletion and setting `"onFailure": "block"`.
Use the same filtered handlers, exiting 2 for deletion and caught exceptions, but leave `onFailure` at its default.
Remove blanket Bash allowance, allow only commands such as `git *`, `npm *`, and `pytest *`, and use `dontAsk`.

questions.explanation:
PreToolUse exit code 2 blocks calls before allow rules. Other nonzero exits such as 1, timeout, or startup failure do not block by default; command/http hooks with `"onFailure": "block"`, from v2.1.295 onward, treat them as blocking failures. Handler `if` filters use permission-rule syntax and start the process only for matching calls. Each `if` accepts one rule, requiring separate handlers per pattern. Failure-safe deletion checks and unaffected unrelated commands are decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Filters run hooks only for deletion-related forms, and fail-closed settings block their failures while leaving other commands unchanged. Tradeoffs are maintaining multiple handlers and unlisted deletion methods bypassing these hooks.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Deletion and hook failures are blocked, but every Bash call depends on the script, so outages block unrelated work.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Filters fit, but default `onFailure` allows calls after startup failure or timeout; internal exception handling cannot cover those.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Allowlists and `dontAsk` avoid deletion/prompts, but reject every new unlisted command, violating unchanged execution of other Bash commands.

**References**: [Hooks reference › PreToolUse › Exit codes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) · [Hooks reference › Handler fields › if and onFailure](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) · [Configure permissions › Extend permissions with hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions)

questions.title: A fixed tool surface for unattended CI
questions.prompt:
A Claude Agent SDK CI code-checking agent allows only `Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`, and `Bash(npm test *)`. Requirements:

- Execute allowed calls and **immediately reject others without prompts**.
- This is read/test work, so **do not automatically approve edits**.
- The CI runner is shared and **not fully isolated**.
- **Do not add and maintain approval callback code**.

Which permission configuration best fits?

options.text: Use `acceptEdits` with the same allow rules, handling other Bash commands through defaults.
Use `dontAsk` with the same allow rules, rejecting unallowed calls without prompts.
Use `bypassPermissions`, listing unwanted editing/shell tools in `disallowedTools`.
Use `default` and implement a `canUseTool` callback that always rejects calls outside allow rules.

questions.explanation:
Agent SDK `dontAsk` executes preallowed calls and operations not requiring approval, such as reads, while rejecting the rest without prompts. Documentation recommends it for headless agents needing explicit fixed tool surfaces. `acceptEdits` autoapproves edits and some filesystem commands; `bypassPermissions` is recommended only in isolated environments. Immediate rejection, no edit autoapproval, lack of isolation, and no new callback code determine the choice.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The allowlist remains, but `acceptEdits` automatically approves file changes.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Configuration alone enforces allowed operations and rejects the rest. The tradeoff is rejection of every unallowed call, potentially prompting workarounds or incomplete checks.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Tool blocking is possible, but bypass mode is intended only for isolation, unlike this shared runner; unblocked tools execute without approval.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Calls requiring approval are denied without a callback anyway, but implementing/maintaining one violates the final requirement. Documentation recommends explicit `dontAsk` rather than implicitly relying on callback absence.

**References**: [Agent SDK agent loop › Permission mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop) · [Agent SDK agent loop › Tool permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop)

questions.title: Managed Claude Code settings enforcing organization-only permissions
questions.prompt:
An administrator deploys Claude Code permissions to all developers. Requirements:

- Apply **only organizational permission rules**, ignoring personal/project allow/deny rules.
- Prevent every developer from **bypassing approval with `bypassPermissions`**.
- Neither policy may be undone by **local configuration edits**.

Choose **two** settings meeting these requirements.

options.text: Commit organizational deny rules in each repository's `.claude/settings.json`, governing edits through code review.
Enable `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` in managed settings, making them the sole rule source.
Copy organizational rules into every developer's `~/.claude/settings.json` through deployment scripts and periodically overwrite it.
Use `--disallowedTools` only when running `claude` in CI and advise developers to use identical arguments locally.
Set `disableBypassPermissionsMode` in managed settings to prohibit `bypassPermissions`.

questions.explanation:
Managed settings have highest precedence and cannot be overridden by user/project settings or command-line arguments. `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` makes managed settings the sole permission-rule source. `disableBypassPermissionsMode` commonly enforces organization-wide bypass prohibition through managed settings. Repository allow rules require workspace trust acceptance, a separate protection. Organization-only rules, no bypass, and resistance to local edits are decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Deny rules precede allows at every scope, but developers can edit repository files and personal rules remain, violating requirements one and three.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Managed settings become the sole rule source and cannot be undone locally.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Developers can directly edit copied personal settings.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: CI-only flags do not affect local sessions, failing organization-only enforcement and bypass prohibition.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: Managed configuration prohibits bypass mode.

**References**: [Configure permissions › Managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions) · [Configure permissions › Settings precedence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions) · [Configure permissions › Project allow rules and workspace trust](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions)

questions.title: Sandbox architecture for executing model-written code
questions.prompt:
An internal analytics agent using OpenAI Agents SDK executes model-written Python against internal data. Requirements:

- Analyses last hours and accumulate files; after human review waits, **resume in the same workspace**.
- Approvals, audit logging, and tracing run on **trusted company infrastructure**.
- Database credentials must **not appear in prompts, instructions, or work files**.
- Use a **managed provider**, as no staff can operate sandbox infrastructure.

Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Use hosted shell, keep approvals/audits on the app server, download artifacts after each request, and reupload them next time.
Use `SandboxAgent`, but run the agent loop, approvals, and tracing together inside the provider sandbox, preserving state through snapshots.
Use `SandboxAgent` with a company-server harness and provider compute, but put DB credentials in workspace-manifest environment variables for direct code access.
Use `SandboxAgent` with a company-server harness and provider compute, inject DB credentials at runtime through provider secrets, and resume saved run state after review waits.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's sandbox guide separates the harness—agent loop, model calls, routing, approvals, tracing, recovery—from compute, where files and commands run. Sensitive authentication, billing, audit, and human review belong on trusted infrastructure. Inject credentials at runtime through provider secrets or mounts, never prompts, instructions, work files, or manifests. Run state, session state, and snapshots are distinct resumption mechanisms. Hosted shell suffices for occasional shell use; workspace isolation and resumable file state warrant sandbox agents. Resumption, trusted infrastructure, and credentials determine the choice.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Hosted shell minimizes operations and keeps approvals/audits in-app, but per-request download/reupload does not preserve the required same workspace.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: One environment simplifies setup, but the guide treats an in-sandbox harness as prototyping; mixing model-executed code with approvals/tracing violates trusted separation.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Harness/compute separation fits, but manifest credentials can leak into workspace code/artifacts.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Separation, runtime secrets, and saved-state resumption meet all requirements. Tradeoffs are provider choice/cost and separately managing run state, session state, and snapshots.

**References**: [OpenAI Sandbox Agents › Harness vs. compute](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/sandboxes) · [OpenAI Sandbox Agents › Trust boundary and credentials](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/sandboxes) · [OpenAI Sandbox Agents › Snapshots and resume](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/sandboxes) · [OpenAI Sandbox Agents › Hosted shell vs. sandbox agents](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/sandboxes)

questions.title: Distinguishing tool visibility from argument-based authorization
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) refund agent has `issue_refund(order_id, amount)`, hidden from ordinary support staff through `is_enabled`. Supervisors now need individual refund limits. Requirements:

- Limits **vary by staff member and come from HR**.
- Determine violations from the tool's **`amount` argument**.
- Enforce limits **independently of prompts**, regardless of generated arguments.

Which addition best fits?

options.text: Split into `issue_refund_small` and `issue_refund_large`, using `is_enabled` by staff grade.
Put individual limits in instructions and tell the model not to call tools above them.
At the start of `issue_refund`, use the staff ID from run context to fetch the limit, compare `amount`, and return rejection without refunding if exceeded.
Make `is_enabled` an async callable fetching limits each turn and hiding refunds for staff with zero limits.

questions.explanation:
`is_enabled` controls model visibility and pre-execution dispatch eligibility. Documentation says argument/resource-based authorization must be enforced inside tools or through guardrails/approvals. Similarly, handoff `is_enabled` runs before arguments are generated, so argument checks require raising an exception in `on_handoff`. The decisive requirements are the `amount` value and prompt-independent enforcement.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Fixed amount-band tools cannot represent dynamically fetched individual limits.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Instructions guide rather than enforce behavior.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Tool-internal comparison of actual arguments and retrieved limits meets all three. The tradeoff is authorization logic spreading across tools, warranting shared helpers or guardrails.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It controls visibility from individual limits, but `is_enabled` runs before arguments exist and cannot compare `amount`.

**References**: [OpenAI Agents SDK Tools › is\_enabled](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tools/) · [OpenAI Agents SDK Handoffs › is\_enabled and rejecting a handoff](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/)

questions.title: Validating model-generated user IDs before ADK tool execution
questions.prompt:
An ADK (Python) agent's `query_orders(user_id, status)` uses a model-filled `user_id` to query orders. Another user's ID could expose their orders. Requirements:

- The unauthorized **query itself must never execute**.
- The server stores the logged-in user ID in session state, **outside model control**.
- Another team supplies `query_orders` as a library, so **its code cannot be changed**.
- The database supports service-account access only.

Which approach best fits?

options.text: Instruct the model to use only the logged-in ID, repeatedly remind it, and inspect responses afterward.
In `before_tool_callback`, compare `user_id` with the session's logged-in ID; return an error dict and skip the tool if they differ.
In `after_tool_callback`, remove rows belonging to other users before returning results and log removal counts.
Modify the tool to call the database with the user's OAuth token instead of a service account, limiting access to user permissions.

questions.explanation:
ADK safety guidance recommends pre-tool callbacks to inspect model-generated arguments when tools cannot be modified, explicitly illustrating `user_id` comparison with the authenticated session user. Returning a dict from `before_tool_callback` skips execution and supplies that result to the model; returning nothing allows normal execution. This requires enforcement data to exist in tool arguments. Query prevention, immutable tool code, and service-account-only access are decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Instructions do not enforce identity, so a wrong-ID query may execute.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It blocks before querying, uses trusted session identity, and leaves tool code unchanged. Tradeoffs are argument-name-dependent rules needing updates as tools grow and agent-scoped callbacks requiring separate installation on other agents.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Filtering hides rows only after the database has already been queried.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: User-scoped access is valid generally, but requires prohibited code changes and unsupported database authentication.

**References**: [ADK Safety and security › Before-tool callbacks](https://adk.dev/safety/) · [ADK Safety and security › Identity and authorization](https://adk.dev/safety/) · [ADK Callbacks › Tool callbacks](https://adk.dev/callbacks/)

questions.title: Global policy through plugins and local argument checks through callbacks
questions.prompt:
An ADK (Python) platform team operates a root and six subagents. Requirements:

- Shared policies such as PII masking apply to **all agents' model/tool calls**, with **one place to change policy**.
- `export_report.destination` must be an internal domain; violations must skip execution and return a model-readable error.
- Only two subagents use this tool. Their owning team **deploys its validation independently**, without affecting other agents.

Choose **two** configurations meeting these requirements.

options.text: Implement common policy in Plugin pre-model/pre-tool hooks and register it once in `App.plugins`.
Copy identical common-policy code into each of the seven agents' `before_model_callback` and `before_tool_callback`.
Attach `before_tool_callback` only to the two exporting subagents, returning an error dict for noninternal destinations.
Put destination validation in the global Plugin's pre-tool hook, conditional on `export_report`, with platform-team deployment.
Implement common policy only in the root's `before_agent_callback`, relying on subagents following the root flow.

questions.explanation:
ADK callbacks are local hooks attached to an agent/model/tool, while plugins apply globally to all agents, tools, and LLM calls managed by `Runner`. Plugin hooks precede agent callbacks; returning a value skips the step and same-point agent callback. A dict from `before_tool_callback` skips tool execution and becomes its result. Documentation recommends plugins for cross-agent safety policies. Global one-place policy and independent owning-team deployment distinguish the choices.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It provides global coverage with one maintenance point.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Coverage is global but seven copies violate one-place maintenance.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Local checks affect only the two tool users and reject execution via a dict. The tradeoff is auditing/maintaining policy across plugin and local callback locations.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Tool-name branching works, but global plugin validation ties deployment to the platform team, violating independent deployment.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Root-local callbacks do not cover subagent model/tool calls.

**References**: [ADK Plugins › Plugins vs. callbacks, Precedence and short-circuiting](https://adk.dev/plugins/) · [ADK Callbacks › Tool callbacks](https://adk.dev/callbacks/) · [ADK Safety and security › Plugins](https://adk.dev/safety/)

questions.title: Introducing approval gates for irreversible actions
questions.prompt:
A team is introducing human approval into a production agent. Arrange five steps so each output becomes a prerequisite for the next.

- (1) Prepare and show an approver a preview containing arguments and impact for each approval-required action.
- (2) Audit-log the approver, time, decision, and execution outcome.
- (3) Classify all agent actions by reversibility.
- (4) Execute approved actions.
- (5) Designate actions classified as irreversible as approval-required.

items.text: Prepare and show an approver a preview containing arguments and impact for each approval-required action.
Audit-log the approver, time, decision, and execution outcome.
Classify all agent actions by reversibility.
Execute approved actions.
Designate actions classified as irreversible as approval-required.

questions.explanation:
Each step requires its predecessor's output. Classification enables approval-target selection; selected targets determine previews. Approvers decide from previews, enabling execution. Audit records include both decision and outcome, so come last. Anthropic's agent-design article describes human judgment at predefined checkpoints or blocked points and recommends sandbox testing and guardrails for high-risk work.

| Order | Step | Dependency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Classify actions | The action inventory and reversibility criteria provide the basis for subsequent steps. |
| 2 | (5) Designate approval targets | Select irreversible actions from classification results. |
| 3 | (1) Show previews | Selected actions determine which arguments and impacts to summarize. |
| 4 | (4) Execute after approval | Execution requires the approver's preview-informed decision. |
| 5 | (2) Audit record | Complete records require both the decision and execution outcome. |

questions.title: Evaluating a programmatic tool-calling design
questions.prompt:
A Claude API team configures `allowed_callers` so `lookup_orders`, `capture_screen`, and `issue_refund` are code-execution-only, then reviews its design. Mark each statement Yes or No.

| Number | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Because `issue_refund` is code-only, the API blocks direct calls, so omitting approval logic from the client's direct `tool_use` path is safe. |
| 2 | Even if code calls `lookup_orders` hundreds of times, intermediate results do not enter Claude's context; only final code output reaches the model. |
| 3 | Returning `capture_screen` as image blocks lets code receive and process it. |
| 4 | If `lookup_orders` results do not return within approximately four minutes, code times out and Claude sees the error in `stderr`. |

items.text: Because `issue_refund` is code-only, the API blocks direct calls, so omitting approval logic from the client's direct `tool_use` path is safe.
Even if code calls `lookup_orders` hundreds of times, intermediate results do not enter Claude's context; only final code output reaches the model.
Returning `capture_screen` as image blocks lets code receive and process it.
If `lookup_orders` results do not return within approximately four minutes, code times out and Claude sees the error in `stderr`.

questions.title: Bash permission matching with wrappers and compound commands
questions.prompt:
A Claude Code administrator is configuring shared project permissions. The sole current allow rule is `Bash(npm run test *)`. Developers often run `timeout 30 npm run test`, `devbox run npm run test`, and mistakenly `FOO=1 rm -rf dist && npm run test`. Requirements:

- Tests, including `timeout` and `devbox` forms, run **without approval prompts**.
- `rm` **never executes**, even with environment assignments or in compound commands.
- `devbox` must not automatically approve arbitrary nontest commands.
- Keep the rule list **as short as possible**.

Which rules best fit?

options.text: Allow `Bash(npm run test *)` and `Bash(devbox run *)`; deny `Bash(rm *)`.
Allow `Bash(npm run test *)` and `Bash(devbox run npm run test *)`; deny `Bash(rm *)`.
Allow only `Bash(npm run test *)` and `Bash(devbox run npm run test *)`; rely on developers rejecting prompts for commands containing `rm`.
Allow `Bash(npm run test *)`, `Bash(timeout 30 npm run test *)`, and `Bash(devbox run npm run test *)`; deny `Bash(rm *)`.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code strips a fixed wrapper list including `timeout`, `time`, `nice`, and `nohup` before Bash matching, so `timeout 30 npm run test` matches the initial rule. Environment runners such as `devbox run`, `npx`, and `docker exec` are not stripped and need rules specifying both runner and inner command. Every compound subcommand must match; deny/ask rules apply to any subcommand, including past leading environment assignments. Absolute `rm` prohibition and restricted `devbox` approval are decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: `Bash(devbox run *)` matches anything after `run`, automatically approving arbitrary commands.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Stripped `timeout` matches the first rule, the `devbox` rule fixes the inner command, and `rm` deny matches `FOO=1 rm -rf dist`, blocking the compound command. The tradeoff is separate rules for each allowed command inside `devbox`.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Unallowed `rm` prompts for approval, but rejection depends on the developer and cannot guarantee never executing it.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Functional safety requirements are met, but explicit `timeout 30` duplicates already-covered wrapper behavior, violating minimal rule count.

**References**: [Claude Code › Configure permissions › Compound commands](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions) · [Claude Code › Configure permissions › Wrappers](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions)

questions.title: Retrying a failed turn without duplicate side effects
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Agents API refund session ends a user-message turn with `agent.session.turn.failed`. The client stream also disconnected midway, leaving it unclear whether the refund tool already ran. Priorities:

- **Never issue the refund twice**.
- **Continue existing work and conversation** stored in the session.
- Recover automatically without people.

Which retry process best fits?

options.text: Leave the old session, create a new one, and resend the entire original user request to restart work.
Reuse the failed turn's `Idempotency-Key` to resend the same message to the same session and wait.
Inspect session/stored items for refund execution, then when `idle`, send a new-key follow-up requesting only unfinished work.
As soon as the session is `idle`, send a new-key "continue" message, checking tool execution only after the response.

questions.explanation:
Agents API recovery guidance says to inspect results after failure, check external actions already executed, and only when the session is `idle` ask it to continue unfinished work. Disconnected streams do not replay missed events; recover state by querying sessions and stored items. Duplicate-refund prevention and reuse of existing work determine the answer.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Restarting without checking previous refunds risks duplication and discards saved work.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, appropriate for a different situation)**: Same-key resubmission retries the same submission after timeouts/lost responses. A follow-up is a distinct submission and needs a new key.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It follows result inspection, side-effect verification, idle waiting, and a new-key follow-up.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Follow-up formatting is correct, but checking side effects afterward allows another refund attempt before verification.

**References**: [Agents API › Errors and recovery › Retry guidance](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/errors) · [Agents API › Sessions › Idempotency keys](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/sessions)

questions.title: Comparing candidates with saturated evaluations and universally failing new tasks
questions.prompt:
A code-fixing agent team must choose between two prompts this week. On 40 existing tasks, candidates pass 39 and 40, providing little separation. Twelve new difficult multi-file migrations were run four times per candidate, and every trial failed. Requirements:

- Keep the existing 40 as **deployment-blocking regression checks**.
- Obtain a **signal distinguishing candidates** this week.
- The **cause of all-new-task failure is unknown**: agent limitations versus broken tasks/graders.
- Run **at most 200 trials daily**.

Which approach best fits?

options.text: Keep one trial per candidate on the 40 regression tasks. Read new-task failure transcripts/graders, fix defects, add stage-level partial credit, and rerun four trials per candidate on each of the 12 tasks.
Keep the 40 regression tasks, discard all-failing new tasks, and choose based on the 39-versus-40 pass count.
Remove the saturated 40 tasks; inspect/fix the new tasks and graders, add partial credit, and run eight trials per candidate on each of the 12.
Keep the 40 regression tasks and increase new-task trials to eight per candidate without investigating causes, watching for passes.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's agent-evaluation article distinguishes saturated capability evaluations, which need harder tasks to reveal improvement, from near-100% regression suites protecting existing capability. Persistent 0% success often signals broken tasks or graders rather than agent limits, so read transcripts. Multistage tasks benefit from partial credit. The decisive requirements are regression coverage, distinguishing signal, unknown total-failure cause, and 200 trials/day.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It retains regression protection, checks defects first, and uses partial credit for candidate differences. Each candidate runs 40 + 48 trials, totaling 176. Tradeoffs are investigation delaying comparison, corrected tasks invalidating earlier results, and team judgment in stage weights.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It meets regression/budget constraints, but one task's difference is weak discrimination and leaves the 0% cause unresolved.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Investigation and partial credit provide signal within 192 trials, but removing saturated regression protection violates its required continued use.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It retains regression checks but totals 272 trials and leaves failure causes unresolved.

**References**: [Demystifying evals for AI agents › Capability vs. regression evals, Partial credit, Read the transcripts, Evals saturate](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

questions.title: Designing evaluations for a customer-facing agent
questions.prompt:
A Claude customer-support team is building its first evaluation set. Constraints:

- **Consistency on the same question** matters most because the agent talks directly to customers.
- Daily evaluation cost limits allow **approximately 100 trials at most**.
- Files/records left by earlier trials **must not affect later scores**.
- Billing, shipping, accounts, and refunds each need **at least ten tasks** to identify branch-specific regressions.

Which design best fits?

options.text: Select ten real-failure tasks per branch, approximately 40 total, run each twice for 80 trials in fresh environments, and report the fraction succeeding both times.
Select ten real-failure tasks per branch, approximately 40 total, run each once in fresh environments, and report pass rate.
Select seven or eight tasks per branch, approximately 30 total, run each three times for 90 trials in fresh environments, and report the fraction succeeding all three times.
Select ten tasks per branch, approximately 40 total, run each twice and report two-success rate, but reuse one environment to reduce setup cost.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic recommends starting with 20–50 real-failure tasks, using pass^k—success on all k trials—for consistency-critical customer agents, and fresh environments per trial. Consistency and isolation are decisive; the daily cap and branch minimum constrain k versus task count. With at least 40 tasks under 100 trials, only two trials per task fit.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It satisfies all four. The tradeoff is weak consistency measurement with k=2; task count and k cannot both grow within the cap.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Cost and branch counts fit, but one trial cannot measure repeated-question consistency.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: k=3 measures consistency more strongly within 90 trials, but fewer than ten tasks per branch weaken required branch-level regression coverage.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Cost/counts fit, but residual state can inflate scores or cause correlated failures.

**References**: [Demystifying evals for AI agents › Start with real failures, pass@k and pass^k, Isolation](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

questions.title: Balancing a one-sided refund-agent evaluation set
questions.prompt:
A refund-approval agent's evaluation set contains only cases that should receive refunds. After a prompt change, scores improved but production overapproval increased. Constraints:

- **Detect overapproval regressions in evaluation**.
- Automate grading while keeping model judgments **aligned with human experts**.
- Valid solutions have multiple tool paths, so **do not mandate call order**.
- Experts have only one day monthly and **cannot grade every trial**.

Choose **two** suitable evaluation designs.

options.text: Pass only trials following the exact lookup → validation → refund tool sequence using a code grader.
Include both should-refund and should-not-refund cases, measuring actions to take and avoid.
Have experts grade every trial instead of using model graders.
Expand should-refund cases into the hundreds for statistical confidence without changing set composition.
Use model grading, checking and calibrating it against expert judgments on a sample of trials.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic recommends balanced sets covering what agents should and should not do, warning that one-sided evaluations encourage one-sided optimization. Calibrate model graders against experts and grade outcomes without rigidly checking tool paths. Detecting overapproval and human-aligned grading distinguish the answers.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Sequence checking works mechanically but fails valid alternate solutions, violating no fixed call order.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Negative refund cases make overapproval visible in scores. The tradeoff is collecting and labeling those cases.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Judgments may be accurate, but expert time cannot cover every trial.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: More examples of the same direction do not detect overapproval.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: Sampled expert comparisons retain automation while reducing disagreement. Tradeoffs are allocating expert time to calibration and periodically rechecking graders.

**References**: [Demystifying evals for AI agents › Build balanced problem sets, Design graders thoughtfully](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

questions.title: Using tool metrics to identify the first improvement
questions.prompt: An internal order agent repeatedly calls `list_orders` with identical conditions within one task and consumes many tokens. Invalid-argument errors are rare, and there is no sign of tool-name confusion. What should be changed first based on this evidence?

options.text: Expand `list_orders` descriptions/examples to clarify argument formats.
Retune defaults such as `list_orders` page size and response-token limits.
Combine lookup tools into one `manage_orders` tool with an action argument.
Add service prefixes such as `orders_` to tool names.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's tool-writing article interprets repeated calls as a reason to retune pagination or token-limit parameters, while frequent invalid arguments suggest improving descriptions/examples. Repetition/high token use and almost no argument errors are decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, appropriate for a different situation)**: It addresses argument errors absent here.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It directly addresses a pattern caused by an unsuitable amount returned per lookup.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, overengineered)**: Consolidation suits fixed sequences across multiple tools, not repetitions of one tool.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, appropriate for a different situation)**: Namespacing reduces selection confusion, for which there is no evidence.

questions.title: Rolling out an agent model migration
questions.prompt:
A customer-support agent will move from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Sonnet 5.5. It forces specific tools through `tool_choice`; every option requires converting this path to `auto` with `strict: true` tools. Preliminary testing shows default `high` effort on 5.5 exceeds the monthly budget. Constraints:

- Switch only after passing **regression quality criteria**.
- Monthly cost stays **within 120% of the current budget**.
- Support **immediate rollback**.
- Release timing permits evaluation of **at most three effort settings**.

Which migration approach best fits?

options.text: Keep default effort, verify regression quality, gradually move traffic if it passes, and retain old settings for rollback.
Compare two or three effort settings including `medium` and `low` on quality/cost, choose the lowest meeting both, gradually move traffic, and retain old settings.
Compare two or three settings for quality/cost, then switch all traffic at once and remove old settings immediately.
Fix `low` effort for cost, deploy to some traffic first, assess quality through production complaints/metrics, and retain rollback settings.

questions.explanation:
Sonnet 5.5's migration guide says identical text uses approximately 30% more tokens than 4.6, adaptive thinking is on by default, and thinking tokens incur output charges, requiring `max_tokens`/cost review. Effort has no one-to-one token-budget mapping, so evaluate two or three levels; `medium` is a starting point for well-defined agentic work. `tool_choice` `any`/`tool` returns 400, requiring `auto` and `strict: true`. Quality, 120% budget, and immediate rollback determine the choice.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Gradual rollout and rollback fit, but default-effort preliminary costs exceed the budget requirement.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Joint quality/cost evaluation selects an acceptable level, with staged rollout and rollback. Tradeoffs are evaluation time across settings and operating both configurations temporarily; if the lowest effort fails quality, rebalance cost and quality.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Evaluation is thorough, but immediate full migration and removal of old settings prevent immediate rollback.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Cost and rollback fit, but production complaints replace predeployment regression qualification.

**References**: [Claude Sonnet 5.5 migration guide › Breaking changes, Thinking runs by default, Effort levels recalibrated, Token usage](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/sonnet-5-5/migration-guide)

After graders reveal failure patterns and criteria stabilize, build a dataset and use eval runs to compare changes.
Make Evals the default starting point even without external-model or large batch-evaluation needs.
Change prompts/tools/routing first, then collect traces and run graders for the first time.

Evals is described for advanced needs such as external-model or batch evaluation. The prompt's first-time adoption is decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: This is the recommended initial stage.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Building datasets/runs before criteria reverses the sequence.

questions.title: Grouping traces for conversations spanning multiple requests
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Agents SDK support conversation spans hours and multiple HTTP requests, with different processes invoking `Runner.run`. Requirements:

- **Group traces from the same conversation** in the dashboard.
- **Filter by application name**.
- **Minimize changes** to execution code.

Which approach best fits?

options.text: Set each run's `group_id` to the conversation thread ID and `workflow_name` to the service name.
Wrap all conversation `run()` calls in one `trace()` block to create one trace.
Keep defaults and put the thread ID in the first line of user messages for later text search.
Disable tracing and store per-thread execution logs in internal storage with a separate interface.

questions.explanation:
Agents SDK `group_id` optionally links traces such as a conversation, while `workflow_name` provides the logical app/workflow name. A `trace()` block combines multiple `run()` calls only when they occur within that block. Different processes and minimal changes determine the answer.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: The same ID groups traces across processes, and the name supports filtering.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: A block groups one code flow; hours of requests across processes make this difficult and require substantial changes.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: IDs contaminate model input and do not use dashboard conversation grouping.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Abandoning dashboard traces fails grouping/filtering requirements there.

questions.title: ADK evaluation metrics that do not require reference answers or trajectories
questions.prompt: A team wants automatic pass/fail evaluation in ADK CI. Responses are open-ended, so there is no expected answer. User utterances vary, so there is no fixed expected tool trajectory. The team needs to check that answers are grounded in tool outputs and that the agent follows stated tool-use rules, such as verifying identity before a refund. Which TWO metrics are appropriate?

options.text: Use only `safety_v1` to assess harmlessness.
Use `rubric_based_tool_use_quality_v1` with a custom rubric describing the tool-use rules.
Require `tool_trajectory_avg_score` to equal 1 for an exact tool-trajectory match.
Use `final_response_match_v2` to measure semantic agreement with a reference response.
Use `hallucinations_v1` to assess grounding in context such as tool outputs.

{{option:C}} and {{option:D}} require references, whereas {{option:B}} and {{option:E}} can assess the required qualities without reference answers or trajectories. These LLM-based metrics require authorization for the Vertex Gen AI Evaluation Service.

- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: A custom rubric can evaluate tool-use rules without a fixed reference trajectory. Rubric quality, model-call costs, and nondeterminism must be considered.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect)**: This requires an expected tool trajectory, which the scenario explicitly cannot provide.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect)**: Semantic matching still requires an expected answer, which is unavailable.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: This evaluates grounding against context such as tool outputs. The tool outputs and context must be retained, and Vertex service authorization must be configured.

(1) Rapid Evaluation; (2) Online Evaluation; (3) Test Case Evaluation

questions.title: Designing pre-change regression evaluation within a CI time limit
questions.prompt: Which configuration best satisfies Requirement 1?
questions.context:
Daon General Insurance, a fictional company, deployed a Google ADK insurance-support agent to Agent Runtime in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and plans to change its model next quarter.

Its existing ADK evalsets cover two kinds of interactions:
- Fixed-turn claims intake, with the required tool sequence `verify_identity` → `open_claim` → `request_documents`.
- Policy Q&A and complaint flows with variable user utterances. Because the utterances cannot be fixed, the team plans to use conversation scenarios.

Requirement 1: Before the change, run regression tests automatically in CI for every PR. Detect violations of the claims-intake sequence deterministically, without judgments varying between runs. CI must finish within 20 minutes. Monitor increased token usage, but do not use it as a pass/fail criterion.
Requirement 2: After the change, continuously detect quality degradation and categorize its causes. Privacy rules restrict access to original conversations to a small number of people. There are two quality staff members.
Security requirement: Minimize the number of people viewing raw customer conversations during evaluation and analysis.

options.text: Use fixed turns for every case with `tool_trajectory_avg_score` and `response_match_score`, cap the number of cases to finish within 20 minutes, and report token usage.
Simulate every case using conversation scenarios and a tool-quality rubric, cap the scenarios to finish within 20 minutes, and report token usage.
Use fixed claims-intake cases with trajectory scoring and simulated conversation scenarios with rubric scoring. Run a large scenario set with generous turn limits on every PR, and report token usage.

Use fixed claims-intake cases with trajectory scoring and simulated conversation scenarios with rubric scoring. Cap the number of scenarios and turns to finish within 20 minutes, and report token usage.

questions.explanation:
`tool_trajectory_avg_score` directly compares tool trajectories without an LLM judge. Conversation simulation is incompatible with `tool_trajectory_avg_score`, `response_match_score`, and `final_response_match_v2`, while rubric-based metrics are compatible. Rubric evaluation uses multiple LLM samples and majority voting, so it is nondeterministic. Efficiency metrics are reported rather than used as pass/fail criteria.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect)**: Fixed responses can cause variable phrasing to fail response-similarity checks and do not satisfy the planned conversation-scenario approach.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect)**: An LLM rubric makes claims-intake judgments nondeterministic, violating the requirement to detect sequence violations deterministically.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect)**: The split between case types is appropriate, but a large scenario set and generous turn limits risk exceeding the CI time budget.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It provides deterministic intake checks, scenario-based checks for variable conversations, a bounded CI runtime, and token reporting. The tradeoff is maintaining two case types and accepting nondeterminism in the simulated-conversation evaluation.

**References**: [ADK › Evaluate Agents › Criteria, User simulation](https://adk.dev/evaluate/) · [Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform › Evaluate agents › Evaluation types](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/optimize/evaluation/evaluate-agents)

questions.title: Continuous production evaluation with limited access to raw conversations
questions.prompt: Which monitoring arrangement best satisfies Requirement 2 and the security requirement?
questions.context:
Daon General Insurance, a fictional company, deployed a Google ADK insurance-support agent to Agent Runtime in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and plans to change its model next quarter.

Its existing ADK evalsets cover two kinds of interactions:
- Fixed-turn claims intake, with the required tool sequence `verify_identity` → `open_claim` → `request_documents`.
- Policy Q&A and complaint flows with variable user utterances. Because the utterances cannot be fixed, the team plans to use conversation scenarios.

Requirement 1: Before the change, run regression tests automatically in CI for every PR. Detect violations of the claims-intake sequence deterministically, without judgments varying between runs. CI must finish within 20 minutes. Monitor increased token usage, but do not use it as a pass/fail criterion.
Requirement 2: After the change, continuously detect quality degradation and categorize its causes. Privacy rules restrict access to original conversations to a small number of people. There are two quality staff members.
Security requirement: Minimize the number of people viewing raw customer conversations during evaluation and analysis.

options.text: Have quality staff manually run Rapid Evaluation with synthetic conversations every morning, without evaluating production traffic.
Continuously run Online Evaluation, group failed evaluations into loss clusters, and validate improvements with CI regression tests.
Run Online Evaluation, then have the two quality staff members read every failed raw conversation and manually categorize it.
Run monthly CI Test Case Evaluation against the production model and treat its score as production quality.

- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: The evaluation modes serve their appropriate roles, and clustering avoids having staff read every raw conversation. The tradeoff is that clusters provide category-level findings; individual causes may still require follow-up investigation.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect)**: The monitoring mode is appropriate, but reading every raw conversation conflicts with minimizing access and burdens a two-person quality team.

questions.title: Agent SDK sessions resumed across days in ephemeral containers
questions.prompt:
A team building a contract-review agent with the Claude Agent SDK shuts down a user's container when the user leaves to save costs. When the user returns, it starts a new container on another node. Conversations resume over several days. The requirements are:

- Resume the conversation context intact, **including tool-call history**.
- Retain project-specific `CLAUDE.md` instructions **after resuming**.
- **Shut down containers when idle**.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Rely on the default session-file location on the container's local disk and try to place returning users on the same node so the files can be found.
Use `SessionStore` to keep transcripts in external storage and resume by session ID, while separately preserving `CLAUDE.md` and artifacts on a shared volume.
Add only `SessionStore`, assuming it also restores `CLAUDE.md` and working-directory artifacts, without separate preservation or synchronization.
Start a new session each time and include a summary of previous analysis and decisions in the first prompt.

questions.explanation:
The Agent SDK hosting documentation explains that session transcripts, `CLAUDE.md` memory files, and working-directory artifacts reside on the container's local disk by default and can be lost when it restarts or moves to another node. `SessionStore` mirrors only transcripts, so the other state needs a separate strategy such as volumes or synchronization. The decisive requirements are preserving tool-call history and retaining `CLAUDE.md`.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: This conflicts with shutting containers down when idle and restarting them on another node. Local transcripts disappear with the container.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It restores transcripts from storage and separately preserves `CLAUDE.md`, satisfying both requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Transcripts are restored, but `SessionStore` does not mirror `CLAUDE.md`, violating the second requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; appropriate for a different situation)**: The documentation presents this as an alternative to session resumption, but it does not preserve the complete tool-call history required here.

**References**: [Agent SDK › Hosting › State that lives on local disk, Session and state persistence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hosting) · [Agent SDK › Work with sessions › Resume across hosts](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions)

questions.title: Isolation and capacity for a long-running agent pool serving multiple tenants
questions.prompt:
A SaaS team self-hosting the Claude Agent SDK serves chat-based analysis agents for multiple customer organizations, or tenants, from one container pool. Users send messages every few seconds, and some sessions use tools for hours, exceeding the target length used in measurements. Each host has 32 GiB of RAM, with 2 GiB of operational overhead. The measured maximum resident memory for representative sessions run to the target length was 1.5 GiB per session. Requirements:

- One tenant's settings and memory files **must not load into another tenant's session**.
- Responses must begin **without waiting for a container to start**.
- Hosts **must not terminate due to running out of memory**, accounting for memory growth as sessions become longer.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a long-running session pool. Set a tenant-specific working directory for every session, leave `settingSources` empty, and apply tenant-specific egress rules. Set 20 agents per host from (32−2)/1.5, cap session length, replace subprocesses, and use consistent hashing on `sessionId` for affinity.

Use a long-running session pool. Set tenant-specific working and configuration directories, leave `settingSources` empty, and set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`. Set 20 agents per host from (32−2)/1.5, cap session length, replace subprocesses, and use consistent hashing on `sessionId` for affinity.

Use a long-running session pool. Set tenant-specific working and configuration directories, leave `settingSources` empty, and set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`. Set 30 agents per host using the starting estimate of 1 GiB per session, cap session length, replace subprocesses, and use consistent hashing on `sessionId` for affinity.

Start a fresh container for every message, restore the conversation with `SessionStore`, and terminate it after responding. Set tenant-specific working and configuration directories, leave `settingSources` empty, and set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`. Set 20 agents per host.

questions.explanation:
The Agent SDK hosting documentation warns that filesystem settings and `CLAUDE.md` memory files can leak one tenant's context into another tenant's session when tenants share a container. In addition to an empty `settingSources` list, it recommends `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`, tenant-specific `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` values, and tenant-specific working directories. Automatic memory is loaded into the system prompt independently of `settingSources`. Agents per host are calculated as (host RAM − overhead)/(per-session RAM upper bound). The 1 GiB figure is a starting point, not an upper bound. Memory grows with session length, so session length should be capped or subprocesses periodically replaced. The decisive constraints are tenant isolation, no startup wait, and no out-of-memory termination.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Capacity calculation and length management are appropriate, but an empty `settingSources` list alone leaves automatic memory and the shared configuration directory in place, violating tenant isolation. Egress rules isolate networking, not settings or memory files.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It isolates settings, automatic memory, configuration directories, and working directories; uses the measured upper bound for host capacity; replaces overlong sessions; and avoids startup waits with a long-running pool.
