questions.title: Daily cost reporting and month-end reconciliation for overnight Agent SDK jobs
questions.prompt:
A team runs overnight batch jobs as individual invocations in the Claude Agent SDK's streaming input mode. Summing result-message `usage` produces a figure below the invoice. Some invocations whose subagents used expensive models crashed, ending with `error_during_execution` results whose cost fields were zero. Requirements:

- Report **cost by model, including subagents**, every morning.
- **Do not omit** the cost of jobs that ended in errors.
- Finance accepts only **figures matching the invoice** at month-end.
- Daily reports are needed the next morning and **cannot wait until month-end**.

Which aggregation and reconciliation approach is most appropriate?

options.text: For each invocation, read `modelUsage` from its latest normal result, or the preceding turn's result if it crashed. Sum by model across invocations, label daily reports as estimates, and reconcile against billed figures at month-end.
Sum result-message `usage` for each invocation to produce daily reports, use the same field unchanged for crashed invocations, and give finance this total as the final cost at month-end.

For each invocation, read `modelUsage` from its latest normal result, or the preceding turn's result if it crashed. Sum by model across invocations and use the same total for daily reports and final month-end costs.
Skip daily reports and reconcile model-level costs, including subagents, once at month-end using billed figures from the Console Usage page.

questions.explanation:
The Agent SDK documentation states that `usage` covers only the main agent loop, while `modelUsage` provides model-level aggregates including subagents. In streaming input mode, each result's `modelUsage` is cumulative for the invocation, so read only its latest result. An `error_during_execution` result after a crash can have zero-filled cost fields; recover from the preceding turn's result. This recovery is unavailable for a single-turn invocation with no preceding result. Costs in `total_cost_usd` and `modelUsage` are client-calculated estimates rather than billing data. The documentation recommends the Usage and Cost API or Console Usage page for reconciliation and financial decisions. The decisive requirements are model-level costs, no omission of failed jobs, invoice agreement, and daily reporting before month-end.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It aggregates costs by model including subagents, recovers crashed invocations from preceding results, labels daily figures as estimates, and uses billed figures for month-end. The tradeoff is reconciliation work when the figures differ and daily reports that are not final costs.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: `usage` excludes subagents, preserving the shortfall against the invoice. It also retains zero values from crashes and treats estimates as final costs.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Aggregation and crash recovery are appropriate, but using client estimates as final month-end costs violates the requirement for invoice-matching figures.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Billed figures are accurate, but skipping daily reports violates both the next-morning model-level reporting requirement and the inability to wait until month-end.

**References**: [Agent SDK › Track cost and usage › Estimates are not billing, Get the total cost of a query, Recover totals after a session crash](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/cost-tracking) · [Agent SDK › How the agent loop works › Handle the result](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop)

questions.title: Recovering overnight batch sessions blocked by unavailable flex processing
questions.prompt:
A team runs contract-processing agents overnight with the OpenAI Agents API. Its 250 sessions use the `flex` service tier, and its budget assumes flex pricing, allowing at most 10% of all turns to use `default` processing. At 02:10, turns in some sessions, representing 4% of the total, failed with `flex_unavailable`. After 30 minutes of retries with backoff, flex remains unavailable with no known recovery time. Before failing, these turns may already have called tools that changed state in an external contract system. About one hour of work remains per session. Requirements:

- `default` turns must remain **within 10%** of all turns.
- Results are due **by 06:00**.
- Contract-state changes already applied **must not be duplicated**.
- Tool-call history must remain **in the same session** for auditing.

Which recovery approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Retrieve sessions and stored items and check applied changes in the contract system. Immediately switch all 250 sessions to `default` in anticipation of a wider outage. Once sessions are idle, send follow-up messages requesting only unfinished work.

Leave failed sessions behind, create new sessions from the same stored agent, and resend the original requests from the beginning. Use `flex` for the new sessions with backoff retries and retain the old histories separately for audit.

Retrieve sessions and stored items and check applied changes in the contract system. Keep retrying `flex` with backoff until it recovers. Once sessions are idle, send follow-up messages requesting only unfinished work.

Retrieve sessions and stored items and check applied changes in the contract system. Retry `flex` with backoff until 04:00. If still unavailable, change only affected sessions to `default`. Once idle, send follow-up messages requesting only unfinished work.

questions.explanation:
The Agents API error documentation recommends retrying `flex_unavailable` later or using standard (`default`) processing for subsequent turns. Failed turns may already have changed files or called external tools, so verify their effects before requesting the same work again. Retries should include waits and an attempt limit or deadline; once the session is idle, send a follow-up requesting only unfinished work. The configuration documentation permits updating a session's model, reasoning effort, and service tier. Changes affect subsequent turns only, and conversation history is retained. The decisive constraints are at most 10% default turns, the 06:00 deadline, no duplicate state changes, and history in the same session.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Effect verification, history, and the deadline are addressed, but moving all 250 sessions to `default` makes default turns 100% of the total, exceeding 10%. Only 4% are affected.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Resending the original request from the beginning can repeat contract-state changes already applied. It also splits tool-call history across two sessions, violating the same-session history requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves duplicate prevention, history, and cost, but waiting indefinitely for flex with no alternative cannot guarantee the 06:00 deadline.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It verifies effects, waits only until a predetermined time before the deadline, and then switches only the affected 4% to `default` if necessary, continuing the same sessions within the 10% limit. There are three tradeoffs: affected sessions remain stalled until 04:00; if flex does not recover, the more expensive default processing increases spending; and applied changes must be checked.

**References**: [OpenAI Agents API › Errors and recovery › Turn error codes, Recovery procedures](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/errors) · [OpenAI Agents API › Configuration › Updating an existing session](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents-api/configuration)

items.text: Sonnet 5.5 rejects `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}`; to turn thinking off, send `{"type": "between_tools"}`.
To reduce latency, it is acceptable to turn thinking off with `between_tools` while keeping effort high at `xhigh`.
Sonnet 5.5 cannot read conversation history containing thinking blocks created by Claude Opus 5, so the request is rejected with 400 unless those blocks are manually removed before sending.
Assistant prefill previously used to guide output format is rejected, so replace it with structured outputs or a tool with an enum field.

This question combines the thinking-configuration and compatibility sections of the Sonnet 5.5 migration guide. Statements 1 and 4 describe documented changes. Statement 2 gets one condition, the effort level, wrong, while statement 3 misstates how unreadable blocks are handled.

1. **Yes**: The guide instructs callers to send `between_tools` instead of `disabled` to turn thinking off. `disabled` is rejected with `invalid_request_error`.
2. **No**: `between_tools` returns 400 when effort is `xhigh` or `max`. Use adaptive thinking at those levels.
3. **No**: Sonnet 5.5 does not read blocks produced by models such as Opus 5, but the API discards unreadable blocks, processes the request with status 200, and does not bill for discarded blocks. No error occurs, but the reasoning is lost.

questions.title: Zero-downtime deployment order with long-running agents in progress
questions.prompt:
A service always has long-running agents working somewhere. It adopts rainbow deployment to move to a new version without interrupting running agents. Arrange the steps in dependency order.

- (1) Confirm that all work in progress on the old version has finished.
- (2) Run the new version alongside the old version.
- (3) Shut down old-version instances.
- (4) Gradually move traffic for newly started work to the new version.

items.text: Confirm that all work in progress on the old version has finished.
Run the new version alongside the old version.
Shut down old-version instances.
Gradually move traffic for newly started work to the new version.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's article about its multi-agent research system explains that code may change while agents are at any stage of processing. Rainbow deployment runs both versions concurrently and gradually moves traffic from the old to the new version without disrupting running agents.

| Order | Step | Dependency on the preceding step | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | (2) Run the new version concurrently | Both versions must be running to divide traffic | Concurrent versions |
| 2 | (4) Gradually shift traffic | The new version must be running before receiving new work | Gradual migration |
| 3 | (1) Confirm old-version work has finished | Remaining work can drain once new work stops arriving at the old version | Avoid disrupting running agents |
| 4 | (3) Shut down the old version | Shutdown is safe only when no work remains | Uninterrupted transition |

questions.title: Choosing an agent loop for a repetitive procedure that does not require judgment at every step
questions.prompt:
Every quarter, Haneul Precision's procurement team runs an agent that retrieves delivery compliance, defect rates, and unit-price changes for 12 suppliers and produces a comparison table and summary. It currently uses a ReAct loop in which a large model reviews the result after each tool call and decides the next action. However, the procedure is almost identical for every request, and retrieval results rarely change the next step. Involving the large model in every call creates substantial latency and cost. The team's requirements are:

- Reduce cost and latency.
- Allow the plan to be revised if a supplier lookup fails or returns unexpected results.
- Keep the structure no more complex than necessary.

Which architecture is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep the ReAct loop and only reduce the maximum number of iterations and output length.

Have a large model create the full step-by-step plan first, then have an executor perform each step using a small model and tools. If a step fails or returns unexpected results, stop execution and have the large model replan.
Assign an independent ReAct agent to each of the 12 suppliers and have them coordinate by exchanging messages.
Have a large model create a plan once, then execute it sequentially to completion. Even if a step fails, leave the plan unchanged and mention the failure in the final report.

questions.explanation:
ReAct repeatedly cycles through reasoning, action, and observation, using observations to determine the next action (the original paper describes interleaving reasoning traces and actions). Its limitations include requiring an LLM call for each tool call and planning only one subproblem at a time. In Plan-and-Execute, a planner first creates a multistep plan, an executor calls tools for each step, and the planner is called again to replan when execution finishes or becomes blocked. It is described as faster and less expensive because it does not call a large model for every action. Deciding who determines each step is central to agent orchestration. This question distinguishes whether the model determines the next action from each observation or follows a prearranged plan. The decisive evidence is [the procedure is almost identical for every request], [the large model is involved in every call], and the requirement to [allow the plan to be revised].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Reducing iterations leaves the large model involved in every call, so the causes of cost and latency remain. Setting the limit too low may instead interrupt valid tasks.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Planning once and executing with a smaller model reduce large-model involvement per call, while a replanning path on failure meets all three requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: Supplier lookups are independent repetitive tasks and do not need coordination between agents. Additional model calls and communication only increase cost and latency.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Creating a plan is appropriate, but without a replanning path it violates [allow the plan to be revised on failure or unexpected results].

Further notes: ReAct is more appropriate for exploratory tasks such as root-cause investigation or web exploration, where the next action strongly depends on the immediately preceding observation. For a mostly fixed procedure with occasional exceptions, as here, planning ahead is advantageous. If the procedure is completely fixed, a fixed workflow without an agent is simpler (see Q04).

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (paper and framework blog) · [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (arXiv 2210.03629)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629) · [Plan-and-Execute Agents (LangChain)](https://www.langchain.com/blog/planning-agents)

questions.title: Designing aggregation when one parallel validation branch fails
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics' customs-checking agent has eight subagents independently inspect eight document types for a shipment, including the invoice, packing list, and certificate of origin, in parallel. An aggregation stage combines their results to decide whether the shipment can clear customs. The document checks are independent. One day, only the certificate-of-origin subagent fails because an external lookup times out. The current architecture starts aggregation only after all eight succeed, so it reruns the entire shipment from scratch. The team's requirements are:

- Reuse the successful results for the other seven documents.
- Retry only the failed branch, up to a specified limit.
- If it still fails, identify which document remains unverified and hand the case to a human so it cannot be mistaken for a pass.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: If any branch fails, rerun all eight checks from scratch and aggregate only the new results.
Exclude the failed branch and issue an overall "pass" based on the seven successful results.
Store each branch result as success or failure and retry only the failed branch up to a limit. If it still fails, label the document "unverified" and send the combined result for human review.
Replace parallel calls with sequential calls, and immediately stop and discard the entire case if any document fails.

questions.explanation:
Fan-out/fan-in splits a task into multiple subtasks and executes them concurrently (fan-out), then collects and combines their results once they finish (fan-in). Orchestration documentation likewise describes waiting for all parallel tasks and aggregating their results. When partial failure affects only some branches, the aggregation stage must know each branch's status (success, failure, unverified) to reuse successful results and rerun only failed branches. The decisive evidence is [the document checks are independent] and the three requirements.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Discarding and rerunning the seven successful results violates the first requirement and increases cost if the same failure recurs.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Issuing a "pass" while omitting an unverified document creates precisely the misunderstanding that the third requirement aims to prevent. Missing documents are particularly dangerous in customs clearance.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Preserving branch status enables reuse and selective retries. Explicitly marking persistent failures "unverified" and escalating to a human meets all three requirements.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, suitable for another situation)**: Fail-fast is appropriate when steps depend on each other and later steps become meaningless if an earlier one fails. Here, checks are independent, so this discards the benefits of parallelism along with successful results.

Further notes: Retry at branch level, but make branches idempotent if they have side effects (see AEP-N14). How partial results are treated—accepted, marked unverified, or treated as overall failure—depends on business risk. For decisions carrying substantial responsibility, as here, marking unverified items and obtaining human review is the default.

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (pattern documentation) · [Durable Functions: Fan-out/fan-in scenario (Microsoft Learn)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/durable/durable-functions-cloud-backup) · Partial-failure handling is general knowledge

questions.title: Protocol versions included in every request under the 2026-07-28 specification
questions.prompt: Haneul Precision's platform team plans to place a Streamable HTTP gateway in front of its internal MCP server so that a load balancer can select server instances using request headers alone. The server and client follow the MCP 2026-07-28 specification. The team is documenting how this specification handles versions. Select TWO correct statements.

options.text: The client negotiates the version through an `initialize` request when starting a connection and omits version information from subsequent requests.
The client includes `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion` in every request's `_meta` and, over HTTP, sends the same value in the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header.

If the server does not support the requested version, it responds with `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` containing the supported version list, and the client may select a mutually supported version and retry.
If the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header differs from the version in `_meta`, the server prioritizes the body value and ignores the header.
Because `server/discover` is optional, a server can conform to the specification without implementing it.

questions.explanation:
The 2026-07-28 specification makes MCP stateless and removes the `initialize` handshake. Each request carries its own protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta`, and the server accepts or rejects it per request. With Streamable HTTP, every POST must include an `MCP-Protocol-Version` header whose value matches `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion` in `_meta`. A mismatch must be rejected with HTTP 400 and `HeaderMismatch`. If the server does not support the requested version, it must return `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` with a list of supported versions (`supported`). The client selects a common version and retries, or displays an error if none is compatible. The decisive evidence is [the load balancer selects using headers alone]: requiring the header to match the body makes it trustworthy for routing.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: The `initialize`/`notifications/initialized` handshake was removed in 2026-07-28. Negotiating and subsequently omitting the version describes earlier specifications (`2025-11-25` and below).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Including the same version in `_meta` and the header on every request is the specification's rule.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Version incompatibility is reported through `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` (code -32022, HTTP 400) and the `supported` list, allowing the client to retry with a common version.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: On a mismatch, the server must not choose either value; it must reject the request with HTTP 400 and `HeaderMismatch` (-32020). This prevents a vulnerability in which a load balancer acts on the header while the server behaves differently based on the body.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Servers must implement `server/discover`. What is optional is the client's advance call to it: the client can send a request directly and retry after an error.

Further notes: A client that also needs to communicate with older servers can use a compatibility procedure: send a modern request first, then fall back to `initialize` if the HTTP 400 response body is not a recognizable modern error.

**Sources**: Evidence type: official (MCP specification, checked at modelcontextprotocol.io) · [MCP 2026-07-28 Key Changes](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog) · [Versioning and Compatibility › Protocol Version Negotiation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning) · [Streamable HTTP › Request Metadata › Protocol Version Header](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http)

Considering Haneul Precision's [Existing environment], [Requirement 1], and [Requirement 2], which combination of integration methods is most appropriate for the three targets: the service portal, label-printing application, and compensation-payment function?
