[Requirement 3] Notes can be edited and deleted, and replacement shipment requests can be canceled in the portal until the logistics partner starts fulfillment. Once approved, a compensation payment cannot be reversed.

[Requirement 4] For compensation payments of KRW 1 million or more, the Finance API requires the authentication event associated with the request token to be within the last five minutes and at a multifactor authentication level. For tokens that do not meet these conditions, it returns an `insufficient_user_authentication` error and the required authentication level (`acr_values`) and permitted elapsed time (`max_age`) in `WWW-Authenticate`, following RFC 9470.

options.text: Operate the portal, label application, and payment screen entirely with computer-use tools. The agent views screenshots and acts with a mouse and keyboard.
Operate both the portal and label application with accessibility-tree-based browser automation, and call the Finance API as a tool for payments.
Use accessibility-tree-based browser automation for the portal, computer-use tools for the label application, and direct function-tool calls to the Finance API for payments.
Defer automation until the portal has an API, and have staff paste screen contents into the agent only to obtain advice.

questions.explanation:
Browser automation reads structured screen information such as the DOM and accessibility tree and manipulates identified elements. For example, Playwright MCP describes operating through accessibility snapshots without screenshots or a vision model and applying tools deterministically using structured data. Computer use generates mouse and keyboard actions from screenshots, so it can also operate non-web desktop applications. However, Anthropic's documentation warns that latency can be slower than manual human operation and that accuracy and reliability have limitations, such as incorrect coordinates. Accordingly, use browser automation where structured access is available, computer use only where it is not, and direct tool calls without a UI where an API exists. The decisive evidence is [the portal exposes accessible names], [the label application has no web interface], and [a Finance API already exists].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: Relying on visual recognition for every target unnecessarily increases latency, tokens, and coordinate-error risk for a portal adequately served by an accessibility tree and payments with an existing API, violating [Requirement 2].
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: The label application is a desktop application with no web interface, so browser automation cannot operate it.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It chooses the most structured available method for each target: browser automation for the portal, computer use only for the non-web label application, and the existing API tool for payments.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: This violates [must work now without waiting for a portal overhaul]. Having a human paste screen contents is not automation.

Further notes: Computer-use documentation recommends running in a dedicated virtual machine or least-privilege container, withholding sensitive data such as login credentials, and obtaining human confirmation for decisions with real consequences. Even if only the label application uses computer use, the isolated environment in [Requirement 2] aligns with this recommendation. See Q14 for a browser-automation confirmation-handling example.

**Sources**: Evidence type: official product documentation · [Computer use tool › How computer use works, Limitations, Security recommendations (Anthropic)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool) · [Playwright MCP (Microsoft) › Key Features](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp)

questions.title: Approval gates and step-up authentication based on side-effect classification
questions.prompt:
Approval gates and step-up authentication based on side-effect classification

In the configuration from AEP-N4, the agent's actions are (a) looking up service cases, (b) adding notes, (c) requesting replacement shipments, and (d) approving compensation payments. Haneul Precision has adopted the principle of "maximizing autonomy while requiring human approval only for irreversible actions." This case involves a payment of KRW 2.5 million, and the approving staff member's token was issued two hours ago after password-only login. Which design best satisfies this principle along with [Requirement 3] and [Requirement 4]?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Haneul Precision manufactures industrial sensors and handles customer after-sales service through its internal service portal. It has three AI engineers.

[Existing environment] The service portal is a ten-year-old web application with no API; it can only be operated through a browser. Its screens consist of standard HTML forms and tables, and each element exposes an accessible name. Replacement shipment labels can only be printed through a Windows desktop application supplied by the logistics partner, which has no web interface. An OAuth 2.0-protected REST API operated by Finance is already available for compensation payments.

[Requirement 1] The agent must look up service cases, add notes, request replacement shipments, print labels, and request approval for compensation payments. The approach must work now without waiting for a portal overhaul and require little staffing and maintenance.

[Requirement 2] The agent runs in an isolated environment. Token usage and latency must be as low as possible.

[Requirement 3] Notes can be edited and deleted, and replacement shipment requests can be canceled in the portal until the logistics partner starts fulfillment. Once approved, a compensation payment cannot be reversed.

[Requirement 4] For compensation payments of KRW 1 million or more, the Finance API requires the authentication event associated with the request token to be within the last five minutes and at a multifactor authentication level. For tokens that do not meet these conditions, it returns an `insufficient_user_authentication` error and the required authentication level (`acr_values`) and permitted elapsed time (`max_age`) in `WWW-Authenticate`, following RFC 9470.

options.text: Place human approval gates on all four actions and call the payment API with the staff member's existing token after approval.
Automatically execute (a), (b), and (c), and place an approval gate only on (d). Treat clicking the approval button as identity verification and call the payment API with the existing token.

Automatically execute (a), (b), and (c), and place an approval gate on (d). If the payment API returns an insufficient-authentication-level error, have the agent use the staff member's stored credentials to complete multifactor authentication on their behalf and obtain a new token.

Automatically execute (a), (b), and (c) with logging only, and place an approval gate only on (d). If the post-approval API call returns `insufficient_user_authentication`, `acr_values`, and `max_age`, ask the staff member to reauthenticate through a new authorization request using those values, then retry with the new token.

questions.explanation:
Classifying actions by side effect makes lookups read-only, note additions and shipment requests reversible writes (editing, deletion, or cancellation before shipment), and payment approval an irreversible change. Placing an approval gate only before irreversible actions fits the principle. Approval gates and step-up authentication are different controls: the former asks whether a human authorized this action, while the latter verifies that the person recently authenticated with sufficient strength. RFC 9470 specifies that a protected resource returns `insufficient_user_authentication` when the token's associated authentication event does not meet its requirements, communicates the needed level through `acr_values` and `max_age` in `WWW-Authenticate`, and has the client use them in a new authorization request. The decisive evidence is [KRW 2.5 million], [password login two hours ago], and [approval only for irreversible actions].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: Requiring approval even for lookups, notes, and shipment requests conflicts with the principle and autonomy requirement. Approval alone also fails to resolve the insufficient authentication level, so the payment call is rejected.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Clicking approval expresses permission but does not create a new authentication event for the token. The old password-login token fails [Requirement 4], so the call is rejected.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Having the agent complete multifactor authentication using the person's credentials undermines the fact that MFA is intended to establish: "the person has personally authenticated now." The person must reauthenticate directly.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Side-effect classification limits approval to payment, while the insufficient authentication level is addressed by following the standard challenge and obtaining a new token after human reauthentication.

Further notes: Q69 covers the sequence for introducing approval steps. The central point here is that approval and reauthentication cannot substitute for each other. Requiring reauthentication proactively at approval time is also possible, but the standard flow follows the requirements supplied by the protected resource.

**Sources**: Evidence type: standards document · [RFC 9470: OAuth 2.0 Step Up Authentication Challenge Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9470.html) · Side-effect classification and the scope of approval gates are general knowledge (see Q69 for the sequence for introducing approval steps)

questions.title: Matching observability terminology to signals
questions.prompt:
An agent operations team is organizing its observability system and wants to select the appropriate term on the right for each of the five situations below. One option on the right is unused.

Situations

options.text: Telemetry
Observability
Logging
Metrics
Tracing
Eval Set

items.text: Alert the on-call engineer if the agent task failure rate over the past hour exceeds 5%. Numeric measurements over time are needed.
Investigate which stages of one slow request—planning, tool calls, or answer generation—consumed time by following their call relationships.
Find text records of individual events containing the error message, input arguments, and timestamp when the refund tool failed.
Find a collective term for data such as logs, metrics, and traces emitted outside the system by instrumentation in agents and tool servers.
Find the term for a system property that enables investigating and identifying the cause of a previously unanticipated failure using only data the system emits.

questions.explanation:
OpenTelemetry documentation describes metrics as measurements of a service captured at runtime, indicators of availability and performance that can trigger incident alerts; logs as timestamped text records; and traces as a request's path through an application. These three—traces, metrics, and logs—are categories of telemetry signals. Observability is the property that allows a system to be understood by asking questions from outside it; it is a system characteristic rather than a tool. The decisive evidence is the key phrase in each situation.

| Situation | Answer | Decisive evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | {{option:d}} | Numeric measurements such as a failure rate over a time window and threshold alerts are uses of metrics. |
| 2 | {{option:e}} | Following call relationships to see where one request spent time at each stage is tracing; an individual segment is a span. |
| 3 | {{option:c}} | Timestamped text records of individual events containing an error message and arguments are logging. |
| 4 | {{option:a}} | Telemetry is the collective term for the logs, metrics, and trace data emitted by a system. |
| 5 | {{option:b}} | Observability is the property of being able to investigate unexpected problems using externally available data. |

An eval set is a collection of inputs and expected results for measuring quality, not an operational signal, so it matches none of the situations.

Further notes: The three signals complement rather than replace each other. Commonly, metrics flag an anomaly, traces narrow down the stage, and logs show its detailed cause. Observability depends on how rich and interconnected the emitted telemetry is (see AEP-N7).

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (OpenTelemetry documentation) · [Observability primer](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/) · [Signals](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/) · [Metrics](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/) · [Logs](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/)

questions.title: Connecting a request trace across an agent and an MCP server
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics' order agent calls tools on an internal inventory MCP server (2026-07-28 specification, Streamable HTTP). A user request took 12 seconds. The agent trace shows an 11-second inventory-lookup tool-call span, but the MCP server records its own traces under separate trace IDs, so they cannot be connected. The team's requirements are:

- Server spans must appear beneath the agent's tool-call span in the same trace.
- Follow the method specified by MCP.
- Do not change tool arguments or model inputs.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Have the agent encode the tool-call span context as W3C Trace Context `traceparent` and include it in `_meta` within the request `params`. The server creates its spans using that context as the parent.
Generate a new correlation ID for every request, add it as a tool argument, and have the server log it so logs from both systems can be searched and matched.
Append the trace ID to the value of the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header and have the server parse and use it.
Start a new trace for every request on the server, but give its spans exactly the same names as the agent spans and match them by name in the dashboard.

questions.explanation:
A trace is a request's path through a system, and a span is a segment of work on that path, with parent-child relationships. Connecting these relationships across service boundaries is context propagation. W3C Trace Context's `traceparent` has the format `version-trace-id (32 hexadecimal digits)-parent-id (16 hexadecimal digits)-flags`. The caller fills `parent-id` with its current operation ID, and the receiver uses it as the parent to create a span under the same trace-id. MCP 2026-07-28 reserves the `traceparent`, `tracestate`, and `baggage` keys in `_meta` for OpenTelemetry trace-context propagation, with values following W3C formats. The decisive evidence is [appear in the same trace] and [follow the method specified by MCP].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Propagating context with the specified key and format attaches server spans beneath the agent span in the same trace without changing tool arguments or model inputs.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, suitable for another situation)**: A correlation ID groups logs and events belonging to one request across systems and can connect logs without tracing. It does not create span parent-child relationships, and changing tool arguments also violates the third requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: `MCP-Protocol-Version` is exclusively for the protocol version and must match its value in `_meta`. Changing it causes the server to reject the request with HTTP 400.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Identical names still belong to separate traces with different trace-ids and cannot become child spans in the same trace. Matching by name is easily confused by concurrent requests.

Further notes: Propagating trace context also enables linking logs and metrics through the same trace-id. See Q80's group_id for grouping multiple requests across one conversation.

**Sources**: Evidence type: official (MCP specification) and standards · [MCP 2026-07-28 Base Protocol › `_meta` › OpenTelemetry trace context](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index) · [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) · [OpenTelemetry Context propagation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/context-propagation/)

questions.title: Designing evaluation when golden-set scores are high but production complaints increase
questions.prompt:
Haneul Precision changes the prompt or model of its IT help-desk agent twice a week. The team measures each change's pass rate using a 200-question golden set and an LLM grader; it has remained at 98% for weeks. However, complaints have increased since a new product launch, mostly about new question types absent from the golden set. For tone evaluation, the grader's agreement with human judgment has never been checked. The team's requirements are:

- Prevent regressions before deployment.
- Detect changes in the production question distribution.
- Check whether the model grader is trustworthy.
- Human-review time is limited.

Which evaluation configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Since the offline pass rate is stable at 98%, attribute complaints to user expectations and continue using the model grader without further checks.
Remove offline evaluation, deploy every change directly to production, and roll it back if online evaluation scores decline.
Replace automated evaluation with humans grading every production response each day.

Retain offline golden-set evaluation as a predeployment regression gate. Run online evaluation on sampled production traffic to detect distribution changes, periodically have humans grade a subset to check agreement with the model grader, and add new failure types to the golden set.

questions.explanation:
Offline evaluation runs a predefined dataset without users and serves as a first defense against regressions before deployment and in CI. However, it can create false confidence if it diverges from real usage. Online evaluation (production monitoring) tracks quality on production traffic to detect distribution changes and unexpected failures. Human evaluation provides the most trustworthy reference but is costly and slow, so it is used on samples to calibrate model graders or establish standards for subjective outputs. These three approaches have distinct roles and do not replace each other. The decisive evidence is [new question types absent from the golden set], [grader agreement has not been checked], and [human-review time is limited].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: New types outside the golden set are invisible to offline scores, leaving both distribution-change detection and grader trust unchecked.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Discovering problems in production without offline evaluation exposes users first, violating [prevent regressions before deployment].
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: Human grading is a reference and a way to calibrate graders; grading everything is expensive and incompatible with the time constraint.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It assigns offline gates, online distribution monitoring, and human sample grading to their appropriate roles, then feeds discovered failures back into the golden set.

Further notes: Anthropic's evaluation article distinguishes automated evaluations for prelaunch and CI, production monitoring for postlaunch distribution changes and unexpected failures, and human graders for calibrating LLM graders. It emphasizes reading transcripts directly to verify that graders work. Q17 and Q83 cover specific configurations on Google's platform.

**Sources**: Evidence type: official engineering blog · [Demystifying evals for AI agents (Anthropic) › Automated evals, Production monitoring, Human graders](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

questions.title: Interpreting A/B results with higher success but lower approval
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics randomly assigned return cases 50:50 between prompt v1 and v2 of its returns agent and ran them concurrently for two weeks. Before the experiment, task success was defined as "closed within seven days without the customer contacting us again." Results are below. Both metrics have sufficient sample sizes.

| Metric | v1 | v2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task Success Rate | 81% | 85% (statistically significant difference) |
| Action Approval Rate (the proportion of the agent's approval requests approved by staff) | 92% | 71% |

The team has a rule: "Approval rate is a guardrail metric because more rejected suggestions increase operational workload." Which decision is most appropriate?

options.text: Hold back a full rollout of v2. Inspect a sample of traces for rejected approval requests to identify rejection reasons and the stages involved, then compare an improved version using the same method.
Roll v2 out fully because the primary success metric increased significantly, and monitor approval rate after deployment.
Treat the success-rate improvement as chance because approval rate declined, discard v2, and end the experiment without further analysis.
Assume staff probably became more demanding and relax approval criteria to bring v2's approval rate back to v1's level.

questions.explanation:
A/B testing randomly assigns variants to real user traffic to compare them, validating meaningful changes with enough traffic. Task Success Rate divides successful tasks by all tasks; its success criteria must be fixed before the experiment for a meaningful comparison. Action Approval Rate measures human approval and signals suggestion quality and operational workload. Even if the primary metric improves, deployment must consider both metrics if a guardrail deteriorates enough to violate the rule. The decisive evidence is [a statistically significant increase in success rate], [approval dropping from 92% to 71%], and [approval rate is a guardrail metric].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: With conflicting signals, hold deployment, use rejected-request traces to identify which suggestions were rejected at which stages and why, then rerun the same experimental design on an improved version.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Full deployment with a violated guardrail increases staff workload first. Postdeployment monitoring reacts too late.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: The sample is sufficient and the difference statistically significant, so there is no basis to dismiss it as chance. Ending without root-cause analysis also loses the elements that improved success.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Changing measurement criteria to match a target distorts the experiment. If criteria need changing, define them before the experiment and apply them to both variants.

Further notes: A/B tests are slow and require enough traffic, so use them for major changes and offline evaluations for routine regressions (AEP-N8). Choosing a winner early after inspecting interim results can mistake chance differences for real effects; define sample size and stopping time in advance.

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (statistical experimental design) and official engineering blog · [Demystifying evals for AI agents (Anthropic) › A/B testing](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

questions.title: Units of agent metrics: Run, Step, and Step Count
questions.prompt: The platform team is defining metrics for its agent operations dashboard. It defines an Agent Run as one execution that processes a user request (one task) from start to finish, and an Agent Step as one cycle within a Run in which the model responds and any resulting tool execution finishes. Select TWO correct statements about metric definitions and interpretation.

options.text: Task Success Rate is the number of Agent Runs judged successful divided by all Agent Runs. A Run still counts as one even if steps within it are retried.

Agent Step Count is the number of steps performed within a Run and should be examined as a distribution (median and upper percentiles), not just an average. Even with unchanged Task Success Rate, an increase may signal rising cost and latency.
An Agent Step is equivalent to one user message, so Run count and Step count are always equal.
A lower Agent Step Count always means a better agent, so the principle is to set the step limit as low as possible.
If tool calls succeed at a high rate in individual steps, Task Success Rate must also be high.

questions.explanation:
Task-level metrics use Runs as the denominator, while metrics explaining cost and latency use Steps within Runs. Mixing units in one system gives the same number different meanings, so definitions must be fixed first. The decisive evidence is the relationship between Run and Step defined in the question.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Task success is calculated at task (Run) level. Retries within a Run do not increase the number of Runs.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Step counts vary across Runs, so an average alone can obscure long Runs such as loops. If step counts increase with unchanged success, the same result is being obtained at greater expense, making this a leading signal of cost and latency.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: A Step is one model-tool cycle within a Run, which typically contains multiple steps. It is not equivalent to one user message.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Required steps vary with task complexity. Arbitrarily lowering the limit interrupts valid tasks. Set the limit using the normal distribution of step counts and use it as protection against runaway execution.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect, confuses related capabilities)**: Tool-call success only measures whether calls finish without errors. A call can succeed even if the wrong tool was selected or its content is incorrect, so it does not imply task success (see AEP-N11).

Further notes: A step limit prevents runaway execution; it is not a success criterion. Q31 covers platform-specific settings for runaway-execution controls.

**Sources**: Evidence type: general knowledge (observability metric definitions; terminology is explicitly defined in the question)

questions.title: Interpreting tool metrics when success is high but responses are slow or wrong
questions.prompt: Nuri Logistics' order agent has a `get_order` tool with a Tool Success Rate of 99.6% (the proportion of calls returning a response without errors or timeouts) and average Tool Call Latency of 0.8 seconds. However, last week it received reports that "responses are occasionally very slow" and "another customer's order information was displayed." What should the team do first to investigate?

options.text: Treat the tool as healthy because its success rate is 99.6% and adjust only the model prompt.

Check latency p95 and p99 rather than just the mean and inspect slow-call trace spans, including arguments and downstream calls. Separately use an evaluation set to verify the content of error-free responses, such as incorrect orders or empty results.
Make the tool return empty results instead of failures to bring the reported success rate to 100%.
Because average latency is 0.8 seconds, lower the timeout to 0.5 seconds to cut slow calls off early.

questions.explanation:
Tool Success Rate measures whether calls finish without errors, not whether the returned content is correct. Even when average Tool Call Latency is 0.8 seconds, some calls can be very slow; the average hides the long tail. Therefore, examine latency percentiles and open slow calls' trace spans to see which downstream calls consumed time. Validate content accuracy with evaluation rather than success rate. The decisive evidence is [99.6% success despite reports of slowness and incorrect content].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: A high success rate does not rule out incorrect content or occasional slow calls. It does not guarantee tool accuracy.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Tail latency (percentiles) and spans address slowness, while evaluation addresses accuracy, matching the two reports separately.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Replacing failures with empty results improves only the metric and hides the cause. The model may incorrectly conclude that no data exists.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: A low average merely indicates that most normal calls are fast. Setting the timeout too low interrupts valid calls and reduces success. Choose timeouts based on percentiles and the normal range.

Further notes: Q76 covers using metrics to identify tools with many repeated calls. This question distinguishes what success-rate and latency metrics do and do not reveal.

**Sources**: Evidence type: general knowledge (metric interpretation) · [OpenTelemetry Metrics](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/) · [OpenTelemetry Signals](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/)

questions.title: Blocking calls to a failing tool API and automatically checking recovery
questions.prompt:
Haneul Precision's after-sales support agent calls an internal inventory API as a tool. Yesterday the API failed, and every call timed out after 30 seconds. The agent retried each call three times, causing requests to take over 90 seconds. Waiting workers were exhausted, slowing inquiries unrelated to inventory as well. The team's requirements are:

- Fail inventory calls quickly during the outage so other inquiries are unaffected.
- Resume automatically after recovery without human intervention.
- Avoid a surge of calls while checking recovery.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase retries from three to ten and lengthen the interval between retries.
Queue requests when an outage is detected, resend all of them at once after recovery, and keep users waiting in the meantime.
Open the circuit to block calls when recent failures exceed a threshold, and keep it open until an operator manually closes it.

When recent failures exceed a threshold, open the circuit and fail calls immediately, returning a tool error or fallback indicating temporary unavailability to the model. After a delay, enter half-open state and allow only a limited number of probe calls; close on success and reopen on failure.

questions.explanation:
A circuit breaker prevents calls that are likely to fail. In Closed state, it permits calls and counts recent failures. Once a threshold is exceeded, it becomes Open and calls fail immediately; a fallback can return a meaningful default if appropriate. After a timeout, it becomes Half-Open and permits a limited number of calls. Success returns it to Closed, while any failure returns it to Open. Its purpose differs from retries, and retry logic must respect an open circuit and stop retrying. The decisive evidence is [requests exceed 90 seconds and workers are exhausted] and the three requirements.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: More retries add calls to an already failing API and lengthen waits, worsening the spread of the outage to other inquiries.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, suitable for another situation)**: Queueing and resending suit asynchronous work that does not need an immediate response. Users are waiting for support, so it violates quick failure and creates a surge immediately after recovery.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Manual-only closure keeps calls blocked after recovery and violates automatic restoration without human intervention.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Immediate failure in Open state contains the outage; limited Half-Open probes check recovery automatically without a surge.

Further notes: For agents, returning a tool error that explains why the circuit is open is important. Otherwise, the model may repeatedly call the same tool or answer without evidence. Sharing one circuit across independent providers can block healthy ones, so separate circuits by resource.

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (design-pattern documentation) · [Circuit Breaker pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker)

questions.title: A job queue that absorbs deadline bursts and isolates unprocessable tasks
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics receives 5,000 nighttime contract-analysis jobs at once, one hour before the deadline. It currently launches an agent instance immediately for every incoming request, but model API throughput and downstream database connections support only 40 concurrent jobs. Exceeding this causes HTTP 429 responses and connection refusals. Several corrupted PDFs also fail no matter how often they are retried, returning to the same queue and delaying valid jobs. The team's requirements are:

- Absorb bursts without losing jobs and process within downstream limits.
- Isolate repeatedly failing jobs so they do not block valid work, while retaining them for investigation.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Autoscale without limits to 5,000 agent instances and process every job concurrently.

Put requests in a durable job queue and cap worker concurrency within downstream limits. As the queue approaches capacity, apply backpressure signaling the receiving side to slow down or wait. Move jobs exceeding the maximum receive count to a DLQ for investigation.
Accumulate requests in the receiving server's memory buffer and silently discard the oldest jobs when it fills.
Keep returning failed jobs to the same queue and retrying until they succeed.

questions.explanation:
A job queue buffers requests and decouples producers from consumers so the service can process at its own pace. This is queue-based load leveling. Increasing consumers without limits simply shifts overload downstream, so concurrency must remain within downstream capacity. Backpressure is flow control that tells upstream systems to slow down or wait when processing cannot keep up, preventing overloading. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) separates messages that remain unprocessed after a specified receive count, retaining them for investigation and reprocessing without blocking normal work. The decisive evidence is [40-job concurrency limit] and [corrupted PDFs returning to the same queue].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Concurrency beyond downstream limits increases HTTP 429s and connection refusals. Unlimited consumers merely move overload downstream.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: A durable queue absorbs work without loss, concurrency limits protect downstream capacity, backpressure signals overload, and a DLQ isolates repeated failures.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Silently discarding jobs from a memory buffer violates [without losing jobs]. Messages must be stored durably.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Returning jobs until success creates poison messages: corrupted jobs circulate indefinitely and obstruct valid jobs.

Further notes: After fixing their cause, DLQ messages can be redriven to the original queue for processing. A DLQ retention period longer than the source queue's is recommended. Monitor queue depth to adjust consumer count or ingestion limits. Because redelivery occurs, consumers must be idempotent (AEP-N14).

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (design-pattern documentation) · [Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/queue-based-load-leveling) · [Amazon SQS dead-letter queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html)

questions.title: Delivery guarantees that prevent duplicate refunds after a worker crash
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Shopping's refund-agent worker receives a message from a job queue, calls an external payment provider's refund API, and acknowledges the message after receiving the response. Yesterday it crashed immediately after the refund call but before the ack. The queue redelivered the message, issuing the same refund twice. The team's requirements are:

- Messages must not be lost.
- The same refund must not be applied twice.

Which solution is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep at-least-once queue delivery and use the job ID as an idempotency key linking the refund call with the processing record. Redelivery of an already processed job does not repeat the external effect, so the effect is applied once.
Switch to at-most-once delivery and delete messages immediately upon receipt.
Enabling only the queue's deduplication (exactly-once delivery) option guarantees one refund even if the worker crashes after calling the external provider, so no additional design is needed.
Send the ack before calling the refund API; if processing later fails, have operators inspect logs and reprocess manually.

questions.explanation:
There are three delivery guarantees: at-most-once avoids duplicates but may lose messages; at-least-once avoids loss but may deliver the same message multiple times; and exactly-once aims to apply the effect exactly once. In real systems, exactly-once processing is commonly implemented with at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer, making duplicate delivery logically apply only once. Because most queue services provide at-least-once delivery, they recommend idempotent consumer logic so repeated processing produces the same result and avoids duplicate records or charges. The decisive evidence is [crashed before the ack] and [no loss or duplicate effects].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: At-least-once delivery prevents loss, and idempotency prevents duplicate effects, satisfying both requirements.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Immediate deletion loses the message if the worker crashes before issuing the refund, violating [no loss].
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Queue deduplication reduces duplicate acceptance or delivery within the queue but does not know that the worker already called an external payment provider. Preventing duplicate external effects depends on consumer and external-call idempotency.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Acknowledging first is effectively at-most-once; a crash before the call loses the job, and reliance on manual recovery cannot guarantee no loss.

Further notes: Pass the idempotency key to the payment API if it supports such a header. If it does not, design processing records written before the call, including an unknown-outcome state. Q72 covers retry procedures using OpenAI Agents API's Idempotency-Key.

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (messaging design) · [Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern › Issues and considerations (Idempotency) (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/queue-based-load-leveling)

questions.title: Checkpointing to resume a six-hour job interrupted by node replacement
questions.prompt:
Haneul Precision's codebase-migration agent performs 40 steps over about six hours. Some steps modify external systems, such as creating branches or opening PRs. If its container is terminated after two hours because a node is replaced, it currently starts over. The team's requirements are:

- Resume after the last completed step following a restart.
- Do not duplicate already-created PRs.
- Do not depend on the container's local disk.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Store only conversation history in an external database, feed it back to the model after restart, and instruct it only to "continue."
Write state snapshots to the container's local disk every 15 minutes.

After each step, checkpoint execution state—current step number, per-step results, created external-resource IDs, and remaining plan—to durable external storage. Resume from the last checkpoint after restart, making resumed steps idempotent by checking external-resource IDs for already-created resources before execution.
Do not store intermediate state; instead speed up step execution to shorten the time needed to restart from scratch.

questions.explanation:
Execution state describes how far an agent has progressed: current step, intermediate results, identifiers of externally created resources, remaining plan, and conversation history. State persistence stores this outside the process in durable storage so it survives restarts. Checkpointing saves state at meaningful points so execution can resume from them. Orchestration runtimes similarly describe managing state, checkpoints, retries, and recovery to run long workflows reliably. The decisive evidence is [do not duplicate PRs] and [do not depend on local disk].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Conversation history is only part of state and does not guarantee reliable records of completed steps and created external-resource IDs. Merely telling the model to continue risks recreating PRs.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Local disk disappears with node replacement, and 15-minute snapshots may not align with the last completed step.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Per-step checkpoints in durable storage establish the resume point, while resource IDs and idempotent execution prevent duplicate PRs.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Without saved state, resumption is impossible, violating the first requirement. Speed improvements do not solve interruption.

Further notes: A crash immediately before writing a checkpoint can cause the last step to execute again, so steps with external effects must be idempotent. Q86 covers the specific configuration for resuming Agent SDK sessions across hosts.

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (durable execution design) · [Durable Functions overview (Microsoft Learn): managing state, checkpoints, retries, and recovery](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/durable/durable-functions-overview)

questions.title: Designing task states and cancellation for long-running work
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics' report-generation agent runs long-running tasks that take tens of minutes. When a user clicked Cancel, the API wrote `canceled` to the task's status field and responded, but the worker kept running. Minutes later it overwrote the status with `completed`, emailed the report, and continued incurring cost. There was also confusion when clicking Cancel on an already completed job changed the screen to "Canceled." The team's requirements are:

- The final status after cancellation must remain `canceled`.
- The worker must stop as soon as possible and clean up in-progress side effects.
- Requests to cancel already finished tasks must be clearly rejected.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a free-text status field that the API and worker can overwrite at any time; cancellation simply writes `canceled`.
Immediately force-terminate the worker process on cancellation and record `canceled`.
Remove cancellation and require users to wait for completion, offering only a button that hides the result.

Define task status as a state machine with permitted transitions only—for example, `working` → `canceling` → `canceled`, and `working` → `completed` or `failed`, with completion, failure, and cancellation terminal and rejecting further transitions. Cancellation moves a `working` task to `canceling`; the worker checks the signal at safe points, such as between tool calls, stops and cleans up, then finishes as `canceled`. Reject cancellation of terminal tasks as "not cancelable."

questions.explanation:
A task lifecycle is the sequence of states from creation to termination. A state machine explicitly defines states and permitted transitions, with code rejecting others, preventing overwrites in long-running tasks whose state is changed by multiple actors such as APIs and workers. Task cancellation is not instant termination: it sends a stop request, and the task cooperatively stops at a safe point. The A2A specification follows this approach: completed, failed, canceled, and rejected are terminal states; the server attempts cancellation but success is not guaranteed; and requests for noncancelable tasks, such as already completed, failed, or canceled tasks, receive `TaskNotCancelableError`. The decisive evidence is [overwritten as completed] and [confusion when canceling completed tasks].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Without transition rules, the worker can still overwrite `canceled` with `completed`.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Forced termination leaves no chance to clean up tool-call side effects, such as partly written files or mail about to be sent, violating the second requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Removing cancellation allows costs and side effects to continue. Hiding a result does not stop the task.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: A state machine prevents transitions out of terminal states, cooperative stopping permits cleanup, and cancellation of finished tasks is rejected with an error, meeting all three requirements.

Further notes: The intermediate `canceling` state is a design choice, not an A2A state name. Add compensation where necessary for side effects that occur before a worker checks cancellation (AEP-N18–N19). States waiting for user input, such as INPUT_REQUIRED, are not terminal in A2A, so define cancelability per state.

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts and official protocol specification · [A2A Protocol Specification › Task states, CancelTask, TaskNotCancelableError](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/) · State-machine design is general knowledge

questions.title: Choosing a configuration by cost per successful task and setting per-task limits
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics tested two customer-inquiry agent configurations on the same inquiry set for two weeks.

| Configuration | Average cost per Run | Task success rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X (small model) | $0.50 | 50% |
| Y (large model) | $0.80 | 90% |

For Y, the 99th percentile of normal Run cost is about $2.50 or less, while rare Runs trapped in tool loops sometimes exceed $20. Failed Runs are also fully billed. The team wants to stay within its monthly budget while preventing a single runaway Run from consuming it. Which decision is most appropriate?

options.text: Choose Y based on cost per successful task. Set a $3 per-task budget cap slightly above the normal 99th percentile to stop runaway Runs and hand them to a human, while retaining a separate monthly budget cap as a safety net.
Choose X because its per-Run cost is lower and set only a monthly budget cap.
Choose Y but set the per-task cap to its average per-Run cost of $0.80.
Choose X and allow unlimited retries until failed tasks succeed to increase the success rate.

questions.explanation:
Cost per Task is average expense per processed task (total cost divided by number of tasks). When comparing configurations, cost per successful task (total cost divided by successful tasks) is more informative because failed Runs are also billed. X costs $50 for 100 Runs with 50 successes, or $1.00 per success. Y costs $80 with 90 successes, or about $0.89 per success. X is cheaper per Run, but Y is cheaper per success. A budget cap limits spending. A monthly cap alone cannot stop one runaway Run in place, so put the per-task cap above the normal distribution and retain the monthly cap as a final safety net. The decisive evidence is the table, [99th percentile about $2.50], and [runaway Runs exceed $20].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It selects Y for lower cost per success, cuts off runaway tasks and hands them to a human, and retains the monthly cap as a second safety net.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: X appears cheaper per Run but costs more per success. A monthly cap alone does not stop an individual runaway Run.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: A cap equal to the average interrupts many normal Runs, whose 99th percentile reaches $2.50, reducing success. Set the cap above the normal distribution.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Unlimited retries increase runaway risk and prevent cost control. Compensating for X's low success with retries further raises cost per success.

Further notes: Instead of simply discarding Runs that reach their limit, designing human handoff or resumption from the same state reduces waste. See Q20 and Q25 for product-specific budget settings and resumption. Step-level caps and period budgets complement each other.

**Sources**: Evidence type: general knowledge (arithmetic and cost-control design; product-specific setting names are not used as evidence)

questions.title: Selecting an overall architecture for cleaning up partial failures
questions.prompt:
Selecting an overall architecture for cleaning up partial failures

Considering Hanbit Trading's [Existing environment] and [Requirement 1], which architecture best handles intermediate failures, including failure at the rental-car step?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Hanbit Trading uses an AI agent to book employee business trips. Each trip calls four separate external systems sequentially: flight booking, hotel booking, rental car, and payment confirmation.

[Existing environment] Each external system immediately commits calls to its own database; Hanbit cannot establish a transaction spanning them. Currently, the agent ends the conversation and reports only "Booking failed" when any step fails. Yesterday a trip failed because no rental car was available after the hotel was booked, leaving the hotel reservation in place.

[Requirement 1] If an intermediate step fails, the system must automatically clean up confirmed bookings. Flights can be canceled free within 24 hours; hotels provide a cancellation API using the booking ID; after payment confirmation, only a refund request is possible, not cancellation. Some fees may remain after cleanup.

[Requirement 2] Cleanup must finish even if calls time out or the agent process restarts midway. Repeating the same cancellation or refund must not cause duplicate cancellations or refunds.

[Requirement 3] Cases that remain unresolved after retries must be handed to staff with visibility into which steps were cleaned up. All calls and logs for a trip must be correlated under one trip number.

options.text: Treat the four calls as one distributed transaction, keeping them reversible until immediately before the last step, and roll all of them back through database rollback on failure.
Retry the failed step until it succeeds and leave successful steps unchanged.

Commit each step immediately in its own system and define an action that compensates its effect: flight cancellation, hotel cancellation, or a refund request after payment. Use a saga that executes these compensating actions for steps completed before the failure.
Have the agent explain the failure and tell the user to cancel each existing booking manually on the respective websites.

questions.explanation:
Work spanning multiple systems can encounter partial failure: some steps succeed while others fail. Rollback discards uncommitted changes within one database and cannot apply to external systems whose participants already committed to their own databases. The saga pattern divides work into a sequence of local transactions; when one fails, compensating transactions undo changes from earlier successful steps. Compensation does not guarantee exact restoration of the initial state; it offsets the failed task's completed work, so fees may remain. The decisive evidence is [external systems commit immediately], [the hotel booking remained], and [Requirement 1].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Each external system commits immediately and Hanbit cannot establish a transaction across them, so database rollback cannot reverse all calls together.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: A failure such as no rental-car availability may not be solved by retries. Infinite retries leave completed bookings uncleared, violating [Requirement 1].
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Local commits and defined compensating actions enable automatic cleanup within external-system constraints. After payment confirmation, a refund request is the compensation rather than cancellation.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Offloading cleanup to users violates [the system must automatically clean up]. Explanation and handoff are a last resort if cleanup fails.

Further notes: Sagas can use orchestration, centrally coordinating an ordered sequence, or choreography, in which participants respond to events. This agent-coordinated case is closer to orchestration (the distinction is general knowledge). Noncompensatable actions such as already-sent email should be deferred to the end of the saga or performed after human approval.

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (design-pattern documentation) · [Saga design pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga) · [Compensating Transaction pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/compensating-transaction)

questions.title: Safely executing compensation and handing off failures
questions.prompt:
Safely executing compensation and handing off failures

Having selected the saga architecture in AEP-N18, Hanbit Trading is designing cleanup execution to meet [Requirement 2] and [Requirement 3]. Which design is most appropriate?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Hanbit Trading uses an AI agent to book employee business trips. Each trip calls four separate external systems sequentially: flight booking, hotel booking, rental car, and payment confirmation.

[Existing environment] Each external system immediately commits calls to its own database; Hanbit cannot establish a transaction spanning them. Currently, the agent ends the conversation and reports only "Booking failed" when any step fails. Yesterday a trip failed because no rental car was available after the hotel was booked, leaving the hotel reservation in place.

[Requirement 1] If an intermediate step fails, the system must automatically clean up confirmed bookings. Flights can be canceled free within 24 hours; hotels provide a cancellation API using the booking ID; after payment confirmation, only a refund request is possible, not cancellation. Some fees may remain after cleanup.

[Requirement 2] Cleanup must finish even if calls time out or the agent process restarts midway. Repeating the same cancellation or refund must not cause duplicate cancellations or refunds.

[Requirement 3] Cases that remain unresolved after retries must be handed to staff with visibility into which steps were cleaned up. All calls and logs for a trip must be correlated under one trip number.

options.text: Compensation must always execute serially in the exact reverse order of the original execution. If one compensation fails, undo completed compensations and restart from the beginning.

Make every compensation an idempotent command keyed by booking ID and durably record per-step progress (success and compensation completed) to resume after restart. Retry timeouts; after exceeding the retry limit, use a DLQ or alert to hand staff the trip number, cleaned-up steps, and remaining steps. Reverse order is the default but may be adjusted to clean up resources more sensitive to inconsistency first.
Treat a timed-out compensation call as successful and record the step as cleaned up.
Have the agent decide which booking to cancel anew from conversation context each time, calling tools without separate progress records.

questions.explanation:
Compensating transactions can also fail and therefore require careful design. Idempotent commands allow repeating a failed compensation without duplicate cancellations or refunds, while recorded progress enables resumption from the failure point. Compensation need not always follow the exact reverse order: some actions may run in parallel or prioritize stores more sensitive to inconsistency. If automatic recovery ultimately fails, manual intervention requires alerts containing the failure reason and a correlation ID such as the trip number. The decisive evidence is [Requirement 2]'s "restart midway and no duplicate refunds" and [Requirement 3]'s "which steps are cleaned up and one trip number."

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Exact reverse order is not mandatory. Undoing completed compensations and restarting increases duplicate-cancellation risk because compensation itself has side effects.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Idempotency, progress records, handoff after retries, and correlation IDs satisfy both requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: A timeout means an unknown outcome, not success or failure. Treating it as success can mark cleanup complete while a reservation remains. Retry idempotently to determine the outcome.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Improvising without progress records leaves no reliable knowledge of completed work after restart, violating [Requirement 2] and [Requirement 3]. Cleanup must execute deterministically through code and state.

Further notes: Free flight cancellation is available only within 24 hours, and hotel cancellations and refunds may leave fees. Do not describe compensation as restoring the original state; report remaining costs to staff. See AEP-N13 for using a DLQ to separate repeatedly failing cleanup jobs.

**Sources**: Evidence type: vendor-neutral general concepts (design-pattern documentation) · [Compensating Transaction pattern › Issues and considerations (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/compensating-transaction) · [Saga design pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga)
